#9613. The Definitive Fine-Tuning Guide for 3D Generation Models

TLDR; In this blog, we provide fine-tuning scripts and containers to fine-tune TRELLIS.2, a popular 3D model on your 3D assets, that can run both locally and on Hugging Face Jobs. If you are interested in fine-tuning, you can use our scripts with few arguments (assuming you updated your dataset to Hugging Face Hub) or tinker with them yourself with this repository. If you want to learn more, we go through how the script works. Let’s go!

3D generation has many uses in robotics, simulation, media, and entertainment. In these fields, it is difficult to make generated objects obey strict rules and standardize model and data representations. There are many file formats, such as GLB and PLY. There are also many representations, such as neural radiance fields (NeRFs) and 3D Gaussian splatting (3DGS). Each one has different advantages and disadvantages.

TRELLIS introduced a common internal representation, called a unified latent representation. Its decoders convert this representation into 3D models in the required output format. Thus, you do not have to use different models for each representation format.

The same team then released TRELLIS.2, which improves the model's representation of 3D structure. But neither model gives an easy way to adapt it to a specific task.

A general-purpose model, such as TRELLIS.2, can make errors in details that are important for a specific application. For example, a user may need accurate geometry for furniture models. Without fine-tuning for that task, the pretrained model can produce geometry that is insufficiently accurate. We use a subset of GSO that has 188 footwear objects for our experiment. In our initial tests, the pretrained model usually produced shoes that looked correct, but the soles were incorrect. We test whether a LoRA can make the soles more accurate.

Our goal is to use the Google Scanned Objects (GSO) dataset to improve the performance of TRELLIS.2 on a specific object category. We will explain which pipeline components to fine-tune and which to leave unchanged during training. The pipeline separates structure, detailed geometry, and materials. Thus, we will fine-tune only the components that are important for our task.

Choosing what to freeze matters as much as choosing what to fine-tune.

LoRA, short for low-rank adaptation, fine-tunes a model by training small adapter matrices while keeping the original weights frozen. This reduces the number of trainable parameters and the memory needed for their gradients and optimizer state. We use Hugging Face’s PEFT library to add and train these adapters. For more information, read our LoRA guide.

Hugging Face Jobs runs containerized workloads on cloud hardware. We use it for preprocessing and for training. To use your own GPU instead, see the local Docker commands below. Before you start, make sure that you have:

Before we train, let’s look at how TRELLIS.2 generates a 3D object and where we’ll add LoRA adapters.

TRELLIS.2 has five main stages: remove the image background, encode the image, predict the coarse structure, generate detailed geometry, and generate materials. The pipeline then exports the result as a textured mesh.

First, BiRefNet removes the background from the input image. DINOv3-L then encodes the image into feature tokens. The generation models use these tokens to guide the 3D object.

The sparse-structure flow DiT predicts the object's coarse shape. It is a diffusion transformer (DiT) that makes a small latent of size 16³ × 8. A variational autoencoder (VAE) decoder then changes this latent into a 64 × 64 × 64 occupancy grid. Each voxel in the grid shows if that location is part of the object. A voxel is a pixel in three dimensions. We add LoRA adapters to this model because its output guides the geometry stage.

O-Voxel is the 3D format of TRELLIS.2. It is a sparse voxel grid. It keeps only the voxels on the object's surface. Each voxel keeps local geometry, such as a mesh vertex, and material attributes. Because the format is small, a CPU changes a mesh into O-Voxel in seconds. A GPU changes O-Voxel back into a mesh in seconds.

Structured sparse latents come from TRELLIS. They keep 3D data in sparse tensors, which makes computation faster. The model uses only approximately 10% of the voxels in the grid, so it does not spend compute on empty voxels. Thus, the shape flow DiT and the texture flow DiT are sparse transformers. The sparse-structure flow DiT is a dense transformer.

The shape flow DiT uses the occupancy grid and the DINOv3 feature tokens to make a latent. Another VAE decoder then changes this latent into O-Voxel geometry at a resolution of 512 × 512 × 512.

We add LoRA adapters to the DiT at this stage because it controls the object's shape.

In the last stage, the texture flow DiT uses the shape latent and the DINOv3 features as input. It defines the materials and textures of the geometry's surface. A VAE decoder then changes the latent into base color, metallic, roughness, and alpha values for each voxel. We do not add LoRA adapters to this stage. Our dataset has diffuse color maps, but it lacks the separate material maps this stage needs for training. Also, our problem is the shoe's shape. The base model already makes good colors and textures.

Finally, the pipeline combines the geometry and material attributes into a textured mesh and exports it as a GLB file.

We add LoRA adapters only to the sparse-structure flow DiT and the shape flow DiT. These DiTs control the object's shape and geometry. We freeze the texture flow DiT to keep its current capabilities.

Our dataset contains diffuse color maps that include baked lighting effects. To train the texture flow DiT, we need separate material maps. The color maps in our dataset mix surface color with lighting. Thus, they are not correct targets for this training.

If we train the texture flow DiT on these maps, it can learn to show lighting as a surface property. It can also forget what it learned before, a problem called catastrophic forgetting.

Our subset has 188 shoes from the 1,030 objects in GSO. For a dataset this small, LoRA is a better choice than full fine-tuning. Full fine-tuning costs much more. It can also overwrite what the model already does well (its learned priors). Our configuration trains approximately 9.3 million adapter parameters in total for both targeted DiTs. We use rank 8 adapters in the attention and feed-forward (MLP) layers of the sparse-structure flow DiT. We use rank 16 adapters in the attention layers of the shape flow DiT. The rank sets the size of the adapter matrices. A higher rank lets the adapter learn more.

A 3D model setup can need many dependencies and installation steps. We supply two Docker images (that you can run on Jobs or your own machine) with the necessary software. One image is for preprocessing, and one is for fine-tuning.

To train your LoRA adapters and upload them to the Hub:

Then we explain the fine-tuning script, its settings, and how each setting affects training.

We’ll walk through three parts of the experiment:

We save the preprocessed dataset so that all training runs can reuse it.

The preprocessing container uses Blender to render 16 views of each object. LoRA training will use these views as conditioning images. Blender runs without a display, through the xvfb-run utility. The container also processes each object through the preprocessing pipeline. See the footwear dataset here for an example intermediate output. For our 188 objects, the full run took approximately 1 hour on an a100-large job. A compact version of the preprocessing pipeline is also available in this companion repository.

For Hugging Face Jobs, we pass the following arguments:

This container accepts a few more arguments (regardless of being run on Hugging Face Jobs or with Docker), that you can find documented over here. The steps taken in the preprocessing pipeline are documented in this section later.

The training container loads the prepared dataset and a configuration preset or file. It records training metrics with Trackio. Use the Trackio dashboard to monitor the run.

We use ‘ss’ and ‘shape’ to indicate the two modes we have for training the LoRAs. The ‘ss’ mode will finetune only the Sparse-Structure Flow DiT, whereas the ‘shape’ mode will finetune the Shape Flow DiT. Under the hood, they simply reference different config.json files to use for each stage. More details about the process is available in this section later.

If you set --push-to, the container uploads adapter checkpoints to the Hub. The container accepts parameters that are also documented here for brevity. A compact script is also available in the same repository.

If you want to play around and fine-tune with the already-processed dataset we have, feel free to use the following set of commands.

The commands and flags are the same as for Hugging Face Jobs. Only the Docker options are different.

If you want to use our already-preprocessed dataset locally on your machine of choice, use the following commands:

Our trained LoRA adapters are in this repository: suvadityamuk/trellis-2-finetune-gso

We use TRELLIS.2’s frozen encoders to convert the input meshes into training latents. We save these latents, so later runs do not have to encode the meshes again.

We also render 16 views of each object in Blender. During training, we select one random view for each sample as the conditioning image. We keep 9 of the 188 objects for evaluation and train on the other 179. These held-out objects show whether the adapters work on objects unseen by the model during training.

Some of the views that Blender rendered for one object

The first snippet sets up the data. FLOW selects the flow DiT to train (ss or shape), and STEPS sets the number of optimizer steps. A batch size of 4 with 4 gradient accumulation steps gives an effective batch size of 16. Then, the snippet loads the LoRA config file for the selected flow DiT, makes the dataset in the TRELLIS.2 format, removes the held-out objects, and makes the data loader for fine-tuning.

We use the peft library to insert LoRA adapters into the selected layers. TRELLIS.2 has a custom forward pass, so the standard PeftModel() wrapper does not work. Instead, we call inject_adapter_in_model(). This function adds the adapters directly to the model and keeps its custom interface.

We keep the trainable adapter weights in 32-bit floating point (fp32) for numerical stability and use bfloat16 (bf16) autocasting for the forward pass. Autocasting lets PyTorch use lower precision for some operations, which decreases memory use. Autocasting does not change how the frozen backbone weights are stored.

It’s important to note that our objective function here is good-old rectified flow matching (as seen in popular image-generation models like Stable Diffusion 3, Flux 2, and others). TRELLIS.2 used the same objective in pretraining, so it is a good choice for fine-tuning. For the theory, read this blog about flow matching.

We update only the LoRA parameters in the sparse-structure and shape DiTs. All original model weights remain frozen.

The snippets below show the core training loop for one stage. They are simpler than the container code and do not include some setup steps. For the full workflow, use the container commands.

We initialize the optimizer and load DINOv3 to extract features from the input images.

We then follow these steps within the training loop:

The training loop computes the loss and updates the adapter weights. Gradient accumulation adds the gradients from 4 small batches before each optimizer step. Gradient checkpointing saves GPU memory by recomputing some intermediate values during backpropagation. The outer loop runs for a given number of optimizer steps, whereas the inner loop accumulates gradients over a set of batches.

For each batch, DINOv3 encodes the conditioning image. For classifier-free guidance (CFG) dropout, the loop sets the conditioning to zero for a random fraction (p_uncond) of the samples. Then, it calculates the flow-matching loss with bf16 autocasting. After the inner loop, it clips the gradients to prevent very large updates and does an optimizer step. It logs the loss every 10 steps and saves an adapter checkpoint every 500 steps.

We trained two adapters: one for the sparse-structure DiT and one for the shape DiT. The LoRA config files in the container image contain the full training settings: ss_flow_lora_gso.json for the sparse-structure flow DiT and slat_flow_img2shape_lora_gso.json for the shape flow DiT. Each run used one A100 80 GB on Hugging Face Jobs. The sparse-structure run took 7.2 hours, and the shape run took 3.6 hours.

The training loss of the sparse-structure flow DiT falls quickly at the start, then more slowly. The loss of the shape flow DiT stays at approximately the same level. These curves show how the training objective changes, but they do not directly measure the quality of the generated geometry.

Flow-matching loss varies with the sampled objects, noise, and timesteps. To find out if fine-tuning improves the geometry, we must also compare outputs on the held-out objects.

The figure below compares outputs for five of the nine held-out objects. It shows the input image, the base model’s generated output, the base output after a rotation adjustment, the output with the footwear adapters, and the reference scan. In these examples, the soles from the fine-tuned model are closer to the scans.

We also use three metrics to evaluate the geometry on the test set:

In the chart’s nine-object comparison, the base model has a mean F-score of 0.276, compared with 0.803 for the model with the footwear adapters. Chamfer distance falls from 0.174 to 0.033, and normal consistency rises from 0.530 to 0.804. With both adapters, the F-score is better on all nine held-out objects.

For the statistics of all runs, see this Trackio space.

Phew, so there we go! We fine-tuned TRELLIS.2 for footwear generation by adding LoRA adapters to the two model components that control geometry. We prepared the data once, trained the adapters in separate jobs, and evaluated the outputs on held-out objects.

The main lesson is to select a training target that agrees with the problem and the data that you have. For this experiment, we fine-tuned the structure and shape stages and froze the texture stage.

Next, we can examine if the same choices help other 3D generation models, such as Pixal3D and UniLat3D.

Gaussian-splat and world-generation models, such as HunyuanWorld 2.0 and NVIDIA Lyra 2.0, are also possible next steps. Their representations and training pipelines can need different methods.

Thank you for following along, and see you in the next one! 👋🤗

#9612. Ai Data Privacy Assessment: Common Pitfalls to Avoid

Understanding common mistakes can help your business to ensure that you implement AI in a responsible manner. This article will look at common mistakes that are made, what impact they can have, and how to avoid them.

Below are some key mistakes to be aware of.

However, there are always changes happening with AI. New features, software updates, more data sets and integration with third parties can cause new risks.

For example, your company may start using an AI chatbot to answer general questions from customers. Later on in the project you may integrate the chatbot with your customer database so it can give personalized recommendations. This could cause more personal information to be exposed.

Some businesses only think about structured data which is stored in databases. They may not consider data from documents, emails, customer interactions, and logs.

This can cause blind spots in your organization. Especially if different departments are using different AI applications. For example, employees may upload customer or business documents to external AI applications without knowing that they contain confidential information.

How to avoid: Ensure that you have a detailed inventory of data. This should include what data is being collected, where it is coming from, where it is being stored, what it is for, and who can access it. Consider mapping out the data flow between the integrated applications to see where personal data is flowing and who can access it.

For example, your company may have a secure way of storing customer records. However, they may be using them to train an AI model without considering if it is allowed.

A common mistake is to just consider your security measures. You may not consider what the external provider is doing with the data.

For example, employees may use an AI writing/analysis tool to process confidential business documents. If you haven't considered how the vendor stores, accesses, and trains their model using the data then sensitive information could be exposed or used in an unexpected way.

How to avoid: Ensure that you complete the correct vendor assessments. Consider what security measures they have, where they store the data, how long they keep it, who they have as sub processors, what they have in their contracts, and if they can use the data to train their model. Regularly review your vendors.

This can impact individuals even if you are following traditional security procedures.

How to avoid: Consider AI specific threats. This includes testing how the model behaves, analyzing the training data, and considering the output. Ensure that you have human oversight for decisions that could have a big impact on individuals.

6. Using incomplete/Outdated Information The accuracy of your assessment will depend on the quality of information you are using. If you are using outdated information, incomplete documentation, or making assumptions about how the AI works you may make incorrect decisions.

For example, your assessment may say that no-sensitive data is being processed. However, after a software update a new integration may have been added allowing the application to access confidential customer records.

Employees may unknowingly share confidential business documents, customer information, or internal communications through publicly accessible AI platforms. They may also rely on AI-generated information without checking whether the output contains sensitive or inaccurate details.

For example, an employee might paste an entire customer database into an AI tool to generate a summary when only a small, anonymized sample is required.

This can weaken trust and create compliance concerns. For instance, a business may collect customer information for account management and later use the same data to personalize AI-generated recommendations without adequately explaining the additional purpose.

Some businesses complete detailed assessments but fail to assign responsibilities, establish deadlines, or allocate resources for resolving identified weaknesses. As a result, important recommendations remain unimplemented.

For example, an assessment may identify excessive access permissions within an AI application. However, if no team is assigned to review and modify those permissions, the vulnerability may continue to exist.

How to avoid it: Organizations should convert assessment findings into an actionable risk mitigation plan. Each identified issue should have a priority level, a responsible team, an implementation deadline, and a method for verifying whether the recommended solution has worked. High-risk concerns should be addressed before deployment wherever possible.

10. Neglecting Continuous Monitoring and Accountability Another common mistake is failing to monitor AI systems after implementation. Businesses may assume that once an application passes its initial assessment, it will continue to operate safely.

How to avoid it: Businesses should establish clear responsibilities for AI governance and data protection. Regular audits, access reviews, system monitoring, and incident response procedures should be part of ongoing operations. Organizations should also maintain documentation of important decisions, system changes, and corrective actions.

Organizations such as Heloixcan also contribute to technology-driven business operations by keeping responsible information management and data protection considerations in focus.

#9611. Sellfy Review 2022: How Good Is This Ecommerce Platform?

 


Are you searching for an ecomerce platform to help you build an online store and sell products?

In this Sellfy review, we'll talk about how this eCommerce platform can let you sell digital products while keeping full control of your marketing.

And the best part? Starting your business can be done in just five minutes.

Let us then talk about the Sellfy platform and all the benefits it can bring to your business.

What is Sellfy?

Sellfy is an eCommerce solution that allows digital content creators, including writers, illustrators, designers, musicians, and filmmakers, to sell their products online. Sellfy provides a customizable storefront where users can display their digital products and embed "Buy Now" buttons on their website or blog. Sellfy product pages enable users to showcase their products from different angles with multiple images and previews from Soundcloud, Vimeo, and YouTube. Files of up to 2GB can be uploaded to Sellfy, and the company offers unlimited bandwidth and secure file storage. Users can also embed their entire store or individual project widgets in their site, with the ability to preview how widgets will appear before they are displayed.

Features

Sellfy includes:

Online Store

Sellfy is a powerful e-commerce platform that helps you personalize your online storefront. You can add your logo, change colors, revise navigation, and edit the layout of your store. Sellfy also allows you to create a full shopping cart so customers can purchase multiple items. And Sellfy gives you the ability to set your language or let customers see a translated version of your store based on their location.

Sellfy gives you the option to host your store directly on its platform, add a custom domain to your store, and use it as an embedded storefront on your website. Sellfy also optimizes its store offerings for mobile devices, allowing for a seamless checkout experience.

Product hosting

Sellfy allows creators to host all their products and sell all of their digital products on one platform. Sellfy also does not place storage limits on your store but recommends that files be no larger than 5GB. Creators can sell both standard and subscription-based products in any file format that is supported by the online marketplace. Customers can purchase products instantly after making a purchase – there is no waiting period.

You can organize your store by creating your product categories, sorting by any characteristic you choose. Your title, description, and the image will be included on each product page. In this way, customers can immediately evaluate all of your products. You can offer different pricing options for all of your products, including "pay what you want," in which the price is entirely up to the customer. This option allows you to give customers control over the cost of individual items (without a minimum price) or to set pricing minimums—a good option if you're in a competitive market or when you have higher-end products. You can also offer set prices per product as well as free products to help build your store's popularity.

Sellfy is ideal for selling digital content, such as ebooks. But it does not allow you to copyrighted material (that you don't have rights to distribute).

Embed options

Sellfy offers several ways to share your store, enabling you to promote your business on different platforms. Sellfy lets you integrate it with your existing website using "buy now" buttons, embed your entire storefront, or embed certain products so you can reach more people. Sellfy also enables you to connect with your Facebook page and YouTube channel, maximizing your visibility.

Payments and security

Sellfy is a simple online platform that allows customers to buy your products directly through your store. Sellfy has two payment processing options: PayPal and Stripe. You will receive instant payments with both of these processors, and your customer data is protected by Sellfy's secure (PCI-compliant) payment security measures. In addition to payment security, Sellfy provides anti-fraud tools to help protect your products including PDF stamping, unique download links, and limited download attempts.

#9610. LLMON: An LLM-Native Markup Language, now in Granite 4.1 3B and 8B

LLMs rely on their context to generate the next set of tokens. Over a long trajectory, the context fills with numerous types of components: a system prompt, past conversation turns, instructions that act on retrieved documents, tool responses or user data, requirements constraining the allowed output, and reasoning chains. The context carries a rich structure, most of which is either implicit to the model or encoded in formats such as JSON that were not designed to be digested by LLMs. This is one of the main reasons LLMs, particularly those on the smaller end of the scale, are brittle and sometimes fail in unexpected ways. The lack of explicit structure can also be exploited by attackers, for example, in the form of prompt injections.

To address this, we developed LLMON (LLM Object Notation, pronounced “lemon”), an LLM-native markup language for explicitly communicating structure and semantics to the models. Semantically coherent components are marked with meaningful tags which are wrapped in reserved special-token delimiters. Data schemas, including nesting, are stated in a way that is unambiguous to a causal LLM. Unique IDs make it possible to point to specific instructions, which could reside anywhere in the context, and bind them to the data payloads they should act on, analogous to the way functions are called and arguments are passed to them in programming languages.

Today we are releasing two experimental preview models, derived from Granite 4.1 base models, trained to consume and generate LLMON-marked text: granite-4.1-3b-LLMON-preview and granite-4.1-8b-LLMON-preview. We are also releasing a GitHub repo, which includes a toolkit for working with LLMON and examples of workflows and templates.

JSON was designed for parsers, not for causal language models. The tokenizer is not constrained to respect the grammar, and structure is encoded by tokens ({, ", :) that may also appear in normal text. To a model, a quotation mark inside a document and a quotation mark that closes a field are the same token. Escaping rules that are clear to a parser are only statistical patterns to a model. Nesting depth is encoded by counting brackets, which transformers are known to be weak at, especially over long spans.

LLMON, on the other hand, is an XML-like markup whose structural delimiters are reserved special tokens rather than characters, so structure and content use separate parts of the vocabulary. Tags are stated at the beginning of each span, and the boundaries between spans are explicit. Nested structures are stated locally so the model does not need to keep track of the hierarchy over long spans.

Since most teams already have pipelines built around JSON, we created conversion tools and example notebooks that translate JSON to LLMON and back in a lossless manner.

LLMON does not replace chat templates; rather, it enriches them. Where regular chat templates tell the model which part belongs to which role (system, user, assistant), LLMON tells it what each component means and how components relate to each other, within and across roles.

The LLMON preview models ship with their own chat template, so you build the same messages list you would pass to any chat model and call apply_chat_template as usual; it renders the LLMON shown below. The only difference is that a turn can now name its parts and mark each one exec: True or False. A part marked True is bound into the exec block at the bottom of the rendered output, which states which instruction to run and what it operates on; a part marked False is still rendered into the context but is referenced by nothing.

Which the model receives as the following (with newlines and indentation added here for readability, as the template emits none):

The two-character block IDs are drawn from a fixed set that this tokenizer encodes as single tokens, so addressing a block always costs two tokens regardless of which ID is drawn.

The role is still a single user turn, but its components reach the model as five separate addressable blocks, bound together by a sixth (the exec block) that states: run this instruction, on this data, subject to these two requirements, and put the answer in the block named here, which is the same assistant block the model then fills. A conventional template would have flattened all components into one string and left the model to infer which part was the task, which was the subject, and which were constraints.

Indirect prompt injection is a type of attack where a malicious instruction is hidden in a data payload, such as a retrieved document, a tool response, or user-provided data. This is the problem LLMON’s instruction/data separation is designed to address.

We compared the LLMON previews against several open-source and closed-source models. We evaluated on the OPI benchmark, which places the injection in the data of classic NLP tasks. Several attack strategies are employed. We report robustness, defined as 1 − attack success rate: the share of attacks where the model does not carry out the injected instruction.

All non-LLMON models are highly susceptible, carrying out the injected instructions with high probability. LLMON practically eliminates the problem on this benchmark, avoiding 47% more attacks relative to the best frontier model that we tested, and 95% more than the best open-source model. We observe similar trends on other benchmarks (ASB and StruQ). It is worth noting that these benchmarks test robustness to static indirect prompt injections. The instruction/data separation directly addresses this type of attack. We are actively working on also improving adaptive attacks which unfold over many chat turns.

Safety gains don’t come at the expense of general capability. Across standard benchmark categories, the LLMON models perform on par with the Granite 4.1 Instruct models.

In short, if you’re experimenting with Granite 4.1 3B or 8B today, you can swap in the LLMON preview and should see comparable general performance with much stronger resistance to prompt injection. No conversion pipeline is required. Naming the turn's parts (e.g., instruction, data, requirement as in the example above) is enough. The shipped chat template turns those into LLMON blocks for you. Our LLMON-converters library goes one level deeper: if a part is itself structured, such as a JSON document, LLMONizing it preserves that structure as typed, individually addressable blocks, instead of one opaque string.

The models start from Granite 4.1 base checkpoints rather than the released instruct models, so LLMON behavior is learned during post-training rather than layered on an existing chat format.

LLMON defines six delimiters that mark the start and end of tags and allow nesting and anchoring; they are installed in the tokenizer as reserved single tokens. We re-serialized a conventional instruction-tuning corpus into LLMON: every prompt component becomes its own addressable block, and each turn carries an execution block naming which instruction to run, which inputs it operates on, and where the output goes. The task mix is the one a normal instruct model sees (chat, multi-turn, RAG, tool calling), which is why benchmark performance stays close to the conventionally tuned model. In addition, we augment the data with decoy instructions and data blocks that are present in context but deliberately left unbound, while the target output is unchanged. So the model learns to follow the dependencies dictated by the execution block and ignore the rest. Reinforcement learning follows: five sequential GRPO stages spanning multi-domain reasoning, RLHF, knowledge calibration, and math, followed by a final DPO stage on a thousand on-policy preference pairs built from the model’s own responses to injection attempts.

The resulting privilege rule falls out of this layout rather than an added guardrail: an instruction reached through an execution block is authoritative, while anything reached as input (data, documents, tool schemas, tool results) is material to read, not a command to follow. Furthermore, instructions and data spans that are not called on in the execution block are ignored. This is a learned behavior, not an enforced guarantee. To see how this plays out in the attention layers of a LLMON model, try the LLMON Attention Visualization on Hugging Face Spaces.

LLMON is not tied to a fixed schema: you can choose tag names and structure that fit your domain and fine-tune an adapter to read and write them. We demonstrate this on ScienceWorld, a text-based benchmark where an agent carries out elementary science tasks (such as boiling water) by issuing one command at a time and receiving a score from the simulator. We defined a vocabulary capturing the structure in the planning trajectories involved in solving these tasks. The vocabulary includes tags such as instr.task.goal, req.planning_policy.rule, data.state.room, data.state.inventory and assistant.next_action. We rendered every step of ScienceWorld's reference solutions with these tags and tuned a LoRA on top of a LLMON model. The trained model then plays held-out games and writes its next action in the new vocabulary. This notebook walks through the full workflow, from converting reference trajectories to playing the test games and scoring the adapter against the untrained base model. Another example for tool-calling agents can be found in this notebook.

This is an experimental preview, ready for exploration and evaluation but not for production.

Tell us what you find: what worked, what broke, and which use cases you’d like to see. Post it in GitHub Discussions.

#9609. How to Evaluate Snowflake Cortex Embedding Models for Enterprise Search

Data engineer, 15+ years. IEEE Senior Member. Researching AI agents on data pipelines; building pipeverify. Writing about the bugs that pass

Data engineer, 15+ years. IEEE Senior Member. Researching AI agents on data pipelines; building pipeverify. Writing about the bugs that pass

Data engineer, 15+ years. IEEE Senior Member. Researching AI agents on data pipelines; building pipeverify. Writing about the bugs that pass

A company has 500,000 support tickets sitting in Snowflake. Years of troubleshooting notes, product defects, workarounds, resolutions, and occasional messages that just say "fixed after restart." Very helpful, thanks.

Someone wants an AI assistant that can search those tickets and suggest resolutions. The architecture looks straightforward. Take the documents, generate embeddings, store vectors, retrieve similar records, and let an LLM write the answer.

A few SQL queries later, you have a demo.

Then someone asks which embedding model you picked.

And there it is. We've designed an intelligent search system using the same decision-making process people use to buy televisions. Snowflake Cortex offers eight built-in text embedding models through AI_EMBED. Some produce 768-dimensional vectors, others 1,024. Some are English-focused. Others support multiple languages. Context windows vary considerably.

I've spent about eight years working with Snowflake, and one lesson from enterprise data engineering keeps showing up: the technically impressive option isn't necessarily the right one for your workload. Embedding models are no exception.

According to Snowflake's AI_EMBED documentation, the built-in text embedding lineup includes:

Snowflake also supports image embeddings through voyage-multimodal-3, but that's a different use case. We're keeping this investigation focused on text.

Eight models sound like eight chances to get it right. Or eight chances to explain to your architect why you chose one based on a name.

A 1,024-dimensional embedding contains more numbers than a 768-dimensional embedding. More numbers must mean more meaning. Unfortunately, vector search doesn't work like upgrading a laptop from 16 GB to 32 GB of RAM.

An embedding model learns a representation of language. Its dimensions are coordinates in that learned space, not a score for intelligence.

A larger representation might capture useful distinctions. It might also deliver no measurable improvement on your particular documents.

Imagine three fictional incident records:

"Why did settlement reconciliation fail after the column changed?"

A useful model should recognize that A and B are relevant, while C is mostly unrelated.

But here's the interesting part. Suppose a 768-dimensional model puts B first, while a 1,024-dimensional model puts A first.

You can't answer that from the dimension count. Maybe both are valid. Maybe one describes the exact failure while the other concerns an older version of the pipeline. Maybe neither contains the accepted resolution.

The model's job isn't to produce a beautiful vector.

For an English-only knowledge base containing relatively short documents, I'd start with a compact model such as Arctic Embed M v1.5 as a baseline.

Then I'd test whether a larger model improves retrieval.

Some tickets are in English. Others are in Spanish, French, Japanese, or a combination of languages.

"El proceso de conciliación falló después de modificar una columna."

"Why did reconciliation fail after the column update?"

Ideally, your retrieval system can connect these without requiring every ticket to be translated first. This is where models such as multilingual-e5-large, Arctic Embed L v2.0, and Voyage Multilingual 2 become candidates.

But multilingual support comes with an uncomfortable question. Does supporting multiple languages mean equally good retrieval in every language?

A model can support multilingual embeddings and still perform differently across languages, technical domains, and query styles.

An error such as ERR_RECON_042 should remain ERR_RECON_042, regardless of the surrounding language.

A model that understands a Spanish sentence but loses the exact error identifier hasn't solved the whole problem. I'd also separate two questions: can the model retrieve semantically similar information across languages, and does the retrieved information actually answer the user's question?

They're related, but they're not identical. Multilingual support earns a model a place in the evaluation. It doesn't automatically win the contract.

Consider a 40-page incident report. It contains the original failure, several failed fixes, the successful workaround, and a postmortem written two weeks later.

A model with a short context window can't embed the whole document in one pass. A model supporting longer inputs gives you more room.

Arctic Embed L v2.0 8K supports longer inputs than its standard version. Voyage Multilingual 2 supports up to 32,000 tokens. At first glance, longer sounds better. Fewer chunks. Less processing logic. Everybody goes home early.

That 40-page report isn't necessarily about one thing.

The first section describes ingestion. The second discusses schema evolution. The third explains a permissions issue. The fourth says the original root-cause theory was wrong. Put everything into one vector and you're asking the model to summarize several distinct concepts into a single location in embedding space.

Now imagine a user searching specifically for the permissions issue.

Will the document-level vector represent that section strongly enough? Maybe. But I wouldn't bet the retrieval architecture on it.

Chunking exists for a reason. Sometimes a focused 300-token chunk retrieves better than an entire document represented by one embedding. Sometimes larger context helps preserve the explanation that a smaller chunk would lose.

The answer depends on the structure of the content.

I'd compare different chunking strategies before spending time arguing about context-window sizes. The bigger window may be useful. It isn't permission to stop thinking about document structure.

One thing I like about the Cortex approach is that generating a text embedding doesn't require standing up a separate model-serving application.

Let's use a small fictional knowledge base.

For this illustrative example, we're calculating similarity against a tiny table. It's not a proposed production retrieval architecture for millions of documents.

More importantly, this SQL demonstrates how to retrieve candidates, not whether the chosen model retrieves the right candidates.

And no, I haven't run this example across all eight models and discovered a secret winner. There are no fabricated benchmarks hiding behind the curtain.

The goal here is to make the model-selection process understandable and reproducible.

Here's my favorite trap in semantic search.

The system retrieves a document discussing reconciliation errors.

The correct document contains ERR_RECON_042, but a different document talks about similar failures in more natural language. The embedding model prefers the descriptive document. Now the LLM receives the wrong evidence and writes a perfectly polished answer.

We've successfully automated being confidently incorrect.

This is why I wouldn't build enterprise retrieval around vector similarity alone. Exact identifiers, error codes, schema names, version numbers, and product IDs often deserve lexical matching. Semantic search helps when people describe the same problem differently. Keyword search helps when the exact characters matter. Both can be useful.

Cortex Search supports hybrid retrieval, making it worth evaluating for applications that need semantic and lexical matching together.

The right question isn't always "Which embedding model should I use?"

Sometimes it's "Why am I asking an embedding model to solve a problem that exact matching handles better?" A screwdriver isn't a bad tool because it struggles with nails.

Let's say you've embedded two million documents using snowflake-arctic-embed-m-v1.5.

Six months later, a new model looks promising. Someone changes the model name used to generate query embeddings.

The stored documents were embedded with the old model. Your queries now use a different model. Even if two models return vectors with identical dimensions, their embedding spaces aren't necessarily compatible. And if one returns 768 dimensions while the other returns 1,024, the mismatch is even more obvious.

So switching models isn't just a configuration change.

You may need to regenerate embeddings for the corpus, maintain parallel indexes, measure retrieval changes, and coordinate the cutover.

This may sound like too much metadata for a vector. Until someone asks why search behavior changed last Tuesday. Then suddenly everyone loves metadata.

If I were evaluating embedding models for a real enterprise application, I wouldn't start with a leaderboard.

I'd start with a set of questions and known relevant documents. For an initial experiment, something like 100–200 representative queries could help expose failure patterns, although broader testing would be needed before making general performance claims.

I'd include straightforward questions, ambiguous queries, similar-but-wrong incidents, multilingual examples, and cases with no valid answer. Then I'd compare candidate models against the same data.

Did the correct evidence make the top five?

How high did the first relevant result appear?

Were the most relevant results ranked appropriately?

How quickly can the model process a search query?

What does it cost to embed the document collection?

How expensive is a future model migration?

What kinds of questions does the model get wrong?

I'd measure actual costs using Snowflake's current pricing and usage information rather than infer them from vector dimensions. And I'd pay special attention to the failures.

Suppose Model A retrieves the correct document for 94 out of 100 questions. Model B succeeds on 96.

A routine FAQ? Or an incident where retrieving an outdated fix could cause another production outage?

Raw accuracy alone doesn't tell you which failure matters more.

That's the problem with declaring winners before understanding the workload.

There's a practical issue worth mentioning. You can have unused Snowflake trial credits and still be blocked from calling certain Cortex embedding functions.

For example, a trial account may return an error indicating that an internal embedding function isn't available. That isn't proof that the SQL syntax is wrong or the requested model doesn't exist.

Account eligibility, regional availability, permissions, and service access all matter. Before writing a benchmark, verify that the account can actually invoke the candidate models. It's a small step that can save an afternoon of debugging the wrong thing.

After looking at the options, here's how I'd approach model selection.

And for every category, verify model availability, pricing, and restrictions in your Snowflake region.

This isn't a universal ranking. It's a shortlist of where I'd begin testing.

Snowflake Cortex makes generating embeddings easy. Choosing the right model is still your responsibility.

Eight models don't mean eight levels of intelligence. A larger vector doesn't guarantee a better match. A longer context window doesn't eliminate chunking. And multilingual support doesn't guarantee that every language or technical domain performs equally well.

A model can retrieve something semantically similar and still miss the evidence your application needs. That's the part worth testing.

If I had to make the decision tomorrow, I'd start with a simple baseline, build a representative evaluation set, and bring in more capable models only when they solve a measured problem.

Because the embedding model isn't supposed to win a beauty contest.

It's supposed to find the right document. And when it doesn't, I'd much rather know that before the LLM writes three paragraphs explaining the wrong answer.

Author’s note: The scenarios and SQL examples in this article are illustrative. They are not drawn from confidential systems, and no comparative benchmark results are claimed.

#9608. actions/cache vs buildx cache: two different systems, measured

Posted on Nov 15 • Originally published at latchkey.dev

The actions/cache vs buildx cache question sounds like a choice between two settings and is really a choice between two systems: actions/cache saves a directory and puts the files back, while a buildx cache backend hands BuildKit layers so it can skip instructions. On one project measured on a Latchkey runner, the first restored an 85 MB dependency tree in 0.374 seconds and the second took a rebuild from 11.9 seconds to 9.4.

The same Node project through each system, from job-k.sh on a latchkey-small runner, 2026-09-20. One pass per row, and the two halves are not alternatives.

Both of these are called a cache, both are configured in a workflow file, and they never do the same job. One is a file-copy service with a key you choose. The other is a store of build results that BuildKit consults while it walks your Dockerfile, keyed on a hash it computes itself.

The confusion costs real time, because the wrong one for a job is not slightly worse, it is useless. So here is what each stores, what each returned on the same project, and the one place they actually collide.

actions/cache takes a list of paths, tars them, and uploads the archive under a key you write. On a later run it downloads the archive and unpacks it back to the same paths. It does not know or care what is inside; a dependency tree, a compiler cache and a directory of holiday photos are the same problem to it.

A buildx cache backend is not a file service at all. It stores the layer blobs and the manifest BuildKit produced, and on the next build BuildKit hashes each instruction, looks for a match, and skips the ones it finds. You never name a key. The build graph is the key.

We ran both systems in one job against one Node project, 414 packages in the lockfile, and recorded what each stored and what each bought back. The dependency side is small and fast: the archive of an 85 MB node_modules tree is 11.3 MB, saving it took 0.322 seconds and restoring it 0.374. The image side is bigger and slower on both counts.

Read the two halves as separate answers to separate questions. Restoring the directory removed a 4.04 second install. Restoring the layers removed 2.49 seconds from an 11.93 second build. Neither number is the other one, and neither of them can be added to the other, because the controls are different: the first is an install with nothing cached, the second is a rebuild on a freshly created builder.

Measured by job-k.sh, under content/repro/timings/actions-cache-vs-buildx-cache/, on a Latchkey latchkey-small runner on 2026-09-20: 2 vCPU, 7,734 MB RAM, Docker 29.7.2, buildx 0.36.1, Node 20.20.2, zstd 1.5.5. One pass per row. The two dependency rows share one control and the image row has its own, so the rows do not add up to a total. The archives were written and read on the runner itself, so they exclude the upload and download a real cache service adds.

Caching a built image through actions/cache is the mistake that looks reasonable: save the image with docker save, restore it next run, load it back. We measured it. The image was 73,041,636 bytes, the tarball 71,344 KB, and compressing that tarball took it to 71,120 KB, a saving of three tenths of one percent, because the layers inside it are compressed already.

So this approach moves about 73 MB through the cache on every run that hits and on every run that misses, and gives you nothing to skip: the image either matches your build or it does not. The layer cache moves 98 MB once and then lets BuildKit skip individual instructions, which is what you actually wanted. Use the layer cache for layers.

From job-k.sh. Saving the tarball took 1.49 s and loading it back 0.80 s on the same machine, so the cost is almost entirely the bytes a cache service would have to carry both ways.

These two systems do not compete until you pick type=gha as your buildx backend. That backend stores its layer blobs inside the Actions cache for the repository, which GitHub documents as 10 GB by default, and which your actions/cache entries are already spending from. On our small project that would be 98 MB of layers beside 11.3 MB of dependencies; on a real image it is the layers that fill the budget.

The failure is silent and it does not look like a Docker problem. GitHub removes the least recently used entries when the repository crosses the cap, so what you see is a Gradle or npm cache missing in a job that never touches Docker. If your image cache is large, put it in a registry and leave the 10 GB to dependencies.

GitHub documents the limit as 10 GB per repository by default, raisable by an owner or administrator, with any usage beyond 10 GB billed to your account. The job needs permissions: packages: write to push the cache image.

The rule is short. If the thing you want back is a directory the next job will read, that is actions/cache. If the thing you want back is work BuildKit would otherwise redo, that is a buildx backend. Nothing you cache with one of them is reachable by the other.

They sit at different points in the job, so the normal shape is both at once: a dependency cache for the steps that run on the runner, and a layer cache for the image build. The only coordination they need is the one above, which is to keep the layer cache out of the 10 GB when the image is large.

Latchkey publishes a swap for each half of that pair, which is the shape worth noticing whichever provider you use. Its documentation says to "Replace the actions/cache step with two latchkey-dev/cache-action@v1 steps, one with action: restore and one with action: save" for the directory half, and latchkey-dev/docker-cache-action@v1 wraps the build for the layer half against a registry provisioned per organization. The documented terms are isolation per organization and a 14-day retention for the dependency cache; no size cap is published, so that is a question to ask rather than an assumption to make.

One script, job-k.sh, run once on a Latchkey latchkey-small runner on 20 September 2026, committed under content/repro/timings/actions-cache-vs-buildx-cache/ with its unedited job-k.log and a status file naming the job id, the runner size and the exit code. The fixture is the same 414-package Node project the earlier Docker measurements used, so the build numbers here sit beside those.

Two things the log does not support. The script also timed a cache export at 4.56 seconds, and that row is not quoted anywhere on this page: it ran on the builder left over from the build before it rather than on a fresh one, so it measured a warm build plus an export and not an export. And type=gha was never exercised, because the log records ACTIONS_CACHE_URL unset outside a GitHub-hosted job, so everything said about it here is from Docker and GitHub documentation read on the same day.

One pass per row, which means a difference under about half a second is not a real difference. That covers the two sub-second archive rows, where the point is the order of magnitude rather than the digits.

Not usefully. It can carry a docker save tarball, which on our project was 71,344 KB and compressed to 71,120 KB, and gives BuildKit nothing to skip. A buildx cache backend stores the layers themselves, and on the same project it took a rebuild after a source change from 11.93 seconds to 9.44.

Yes. It stores its layer blobs in the Actions cache for the repository, which shares the documented 10 GB default with every actions/cache entry you keep. The symptom of crowding it out is a dependency cache missing in a job that has nothing to do with Docker, because GitHub evicts the least recently used entries once the repository crosses the cap.

For a large image, yes, mostly because of where the bytes live. A registry cache costs registry storage and credentials and leaves the 10 GB repository budget to dependencies, and it can be shared across repositories. For a small image type=gha needs no setup at all, which is a real advantage while the cache stays small.

If your job both installs dependencies on the runner and builds an image, yes, because they skip different work. Our measurements put the dependency restore at 0.374 seconds against a 4.04 second install, and the layer cache at 2.49 seconds off an 11.93 second build. Neither one covers the other.

#9607. Your agent's token bill is mostly the same prompt, sent again

Most of what you pay for when an agent works is the same text, sent again.

Every time an agent thinks, the whole prompt goes back to the model: its instructions, its tool definitions, the conversation so far. On a long task that repeated part is the majority of the bill. Providers know this and sell a discount on it called prompt caching — but the discount only applies if the start of the prompt is byte-for-byte identical to last time. Change one character near the top and you pay full price for everything after it.

That sounds like a small implementation detail. It is the single biggest lever on what an agent costs to run, and most agent frameworks lose it by accident.

The cache is a prefix match. Anything that varies at the top of the prompt invalidates everything below it. The usual culprits:

None of these look like a cost decision when you write them. All of them are.

The clearest example I know is in OpenClaw's own issue tracker: an open report that heartbeats put the current time into the cached start of the prompt, so each heartbeat pays to write the cache again instead of reading it. A heartbeat is supposed to be the cheapest thing an agent does — wake up, check nothing needs attention, go back to sleep. If the clock sits in the cached prefix, every one of those wake-ups is a full-price prompt write.

The fix is not clever. It is discipline about what goes at the top.

1. The system prompt is byte-identical every turn. Persona, instructions, skills — no clock, no counters, no "you have 3 tasks remaining". If the agent needs to know the time, it calls a tool and the answer lands in the conversation, below the cached part.

2. History only grows at the end. Old messages are replayed exactly as they were, stamped with the time they arrived, never re-stamped. Appending is free; rewriting is not.

3. Summarise once, don't trim every turn. When a conversation gets long, compact it once and then let it grow at the end again. Dropping one old message per turn means the prefix changes on every call, which means you never get a cache hit at all.

4. Waiting costs nothing. An agent blocked on a colleague, a timer or a build should make zero model calls until something arrives. This is the one people miss, because a polling loop feels harmless — it is a full prompt every few seconds.

Take an agent whose instructions, tools and history add up to 30,000 tokens, making 20 model calls on a task.

Sent uncached, that is 600,000 input tokens at full price.

At typical cached-input pricing, where a cache read costs roughly a tenth of normal input, the first call writes the cache and the other 19 read it. That is about 85% less on the repeated part — and the repeated part is most of the bill.

The same arithmetic applies to specialists. A sub-agent that starts with its own short brief instead of inheriting the parent's whole conversation is cheaper on every call it makes, and it can run on a smaller model without losing anything, because it only has one job.

Caching is also why the subscription question keeps coming up. In April 2026 Anthropic stopped letting Claude Pro and Max subscriptions cover third-party agent tools, citing its terms of service and load on its systems; in May it let them back in on a separate monthly credit. If you are running an agent on a flat-rate subscription, your cost model depends on a policy someone else can change, and the caching behaviour underneath it is not yours to control.

If you are building this yourself, the four rules above are most of the work, and they are worth more than any model upgrade.

I work on AgentParley, a hosted platform for crews of AI agents. We build every prompt so the repeated part stays byte-identical, which is where the numbers above come from. If you want the longer version, including how it compares to self-hosting, there is a full comparison here.

llama.cpp makes it possible to run multi-modal LLMs across a wide range of hardware - from consumer-grade local machines to high-end enterprise servers. Through quantization, optimized backends, and a portable C/C++ implementation, we make AI inference accessible at every level of the software stack. We believe this is the most lightweight, versatile and sensible platform for building cross-platform and private AI products.

Today we release libraries v1.0.0, highlighting our responsibility to those developers. Moving forward, both llama.cpp and ggml will reflect API and ABI incompatibilities with major-version bumps. As adoption grows, we will be stricter about making those boundaries visible to downstream consumers.

The following rules apply to all ggml-org projects using semantic versioning:

We are looking forward to expanding the ways in which ggml-org software is distributed and reaches developers and end-users. For more information about how to add ggml-org projects to your packaging and release pipelines, please check the following discussion.

The project has fostered an amazing open-source community with highly-skilled and talented contributors. With the rapid advance of AI capabilities in the field of software engineering, we continue to adapt and integrate LLMs in our developement cycle in a thoughtful and resonable manner. Maintaining a high quality codebase, staying in control of the architecture and understanding the implementation details will remain our top priorities.

To reinforce the faster pace of development we continue to invest more and more resources in improving the CI infrastructure behind the projects. Thanks to HF technologies such as HF Buckets and HF Jobs we are able to scale the capacity necessary to guarantee correctness for every change that lands on the master branches. With hardware support from NVIDIA, AMD, Qualcomm, Arm, IBM and Intel, we continue to enroll more self-hosted runners across all major hardware platforms.

The underlying machine learning engine of llama.cpp - ggml is designed to run on virtually any hardware in existence. This is achieved by implementing dedicated ggml backends. Each backend can be compiled as a dynamic library and optionally loaded at runtime.

A complete list of the currently implemented backends can be found here.

We are committed to provide continuous support of all model architectures. Currently, llama.cpp supports more than 150 architecture variants as well as all mainstream speculative decoding methods.

The llama.cpp team at Hugging Face is thankful for the incredible support from the community. Special thanks to the long-time maintainers of the project and all contributors. This is a significant milestone which would not have been possible without our joint efforts!

#9605. ProWritingAid VS Grammarly: Which Grammar Checker is Better in (2022) ?

ProWritingAid VS Grammarly:  When it comes to English grammar, there are two Big Players that everyone knows of: the Grammarly and ProWritingAid. but you are wondering which one to choose so here we write a detail article which will help you to choose the best one for you so Let's start

What is Grammarly?

Grammarly is a tool that checks for grammatical errors, spelling, and punctuation.it gives you comprehensive feedback on your writing. You can use this tool to proofread and edit articles, blog posts, emails, etc.

Grammarly also detects all types of mistakes, including sentence structure issues and misused words. It also gives you suggestions on style changes, punctuation, spelling, and grammar all are in real-time. The free version covers the basics like identifying grammar and spelling mistakes

whereas the Premium version offers a lot more functionality, it detects plagiarism in your content, suggests word choice, or adds fluency to it.


Features of Grammarly

  • Spelling and Word Suggestion: Grammarly detects basic to advance grammatical errors and also help you why this is an error and suggest to you how you can improve it
  • Create a Personal Dictionary: The Grammarly app allows you to add words to your personal dictionary so that the same mistake isn't highlighted every time you run Grammarly.
  • Different English Style: Check to spell for American, British, Canadian, and Australian English.
  • Plagiarism: This feature helps you detect if a text has been plagiarized by comparing it with over eight billion web pages.
  • Wordiness: This tool will help you check your writing for long and hard-to-read sentences. It also shows you how to shorten sentences so that they are more concise.
  • Passive Voice: The program also notifies users when passive voice is used too frequently in a document.
  • Punctuations: This feature flags all incorrect and missing punctuation.
  • Repetition: The tool provides recommendations for replacing the repeated word.
  • Proposition: Grammarly identifies misplaced and confused prepositions.

  • Plugins: It offers Microsoft Word, Microsoft Outlook, and Google Chrome plugins.


What is ProWritingAid?

ProWritingAid is a style and grammar checker for content creators and writers. It helps to optimize word choice, punctuation errors, and common grammar mistakes, providing detailed reports to help you improve your writing. 

ProWritingAid can be used as an add-on to WordPress, Gmail, and Google Docs. The software also offers helpful articles, videos, quizzes, and explanations to help improve your writing.

Features of ProWriting Aid

Here are some key features of ProWriting Aid:

  • Grammar checker and spell checker: This tool helps you to find all grammatical and spelling errors.
  • Find repeated words:  The tool also allows you to search for repeated words and phrases in your content.
  • Context-sensitive style suggestions:  You can find the exact style of writing you intend and suggest if it flows well in your writing.
  • Check the readability of your content: Pro Writing Aid helps you identify the strengths and weaknesses of your article by pointing out difficult sentences and paragraphs.
  • Sentence Length: It also indicates the length of your sentences.
  • Check Grammatical error: It also checks your work for any grammatical errors or typos, as well.
  • Overused words: As a writer, you might find yourself using the same word repeatedly. ProWritingAid's overused words checker helps you avoid this lazy writing mistake.
  • Consistency: Check your work for inconsistent usage of open and closed quotation marks.
  • Echoes: Check your writing for uniformly repetitive words and phrases.

Difference between Grammarly and Pro-Writing Aid

Grammarly and ProWritingAid are well-known grammar-checking software. However, if you're like most people who can't decide which to use, here are some different points that may be helpful in your decision.

Grammarly vs ProWritingAid

  • Grammarly is a writing enhancement tool that offers suggestions for grammar, vocabulary, and syntax whereas ProWritingAid offers world-class grammar and style checking, as well as advanced reports to help you strengthen your writing.
  • Grammarly provides Android and IOS apps whereas ProWritingAid doesn't have a mobile or IOS app.
  • Grammarly offers important suggestions about mistakes you've made whereas ProWritingAid  shows more suggestions than Grammarly but all recommendations are not accurate
  • Grammarly has a more friendly UI/UX whereas the ProWritingAid interface is not friendly as Grammarly.
  • Grammarly is an accurate grammar checker for non-fiction writing whereas ProWritingAid is an accurate grammar checker for fiction writers.
  • Grammarly finds grammar and punctuation mistakes, whereas ProWritingAid identifies run-on sentences and fragments.
  • Grammarly provides 24/7 support via submitting a ticket and sending emails. ProWritingAid’s support team is available via email, though the response time is approximately 48 hours.
  • Grammarly offers many features in its free plan, whereas ProWritingAid offers some basic features in the free plan.
  • Grammarly does not offer much feedback on big picture writing; ProWritingAid offers complete feedback on big picture writing.
  • Grammarly is a better option for accuracy, whereas ProWritingAid is better for handling fragmented sentences and dialogue. It can be quite useful for fiction writers.

ProWritingAid VS Grammarly: Pricing Difference

  • ProWritingAid comes with three pricing structures. The full-year cost of ProWritingAid is $79, while its lifetime plans cost $339. You also can opt for a monthly plan of $20.
  • Grammarly offers a Premium subscription for $30/month for a monthly plan  $20/month for quarterly and $12/month for an annual subscription.
  • The Business plan costs $12.50 per month for each member of your company.

ProWritingAid vs Grammarly – Pros and Cons

Grammarly Pros

  • It allows you to fix common mistakes like grammar and spelling.
  • Offers most features in the free plan
  • Allows you to edit a document without affecting the formatting.
  • Active and passive voice checker
  • Personal dictionary 
  • Plagiarism checker (paid version)
  • Proofread your writing and correct all punctuation, grammar, and spelling errors.
  • Allows you to make changes to a document without altering its formatting.
  • Helps users improve vocabulary
  • User-friendly interface
  • Browser extensions and MS word add-ons
  • Available on all major devices and platforms
  • Grammarly will also offer suggestions to improve your style.
  • Enhance the readability of your sentence
  • Free mobile apps 
  • Offers  free version

Grammarly Cons

  • Supports only English 
  • Customer support only via email
  • Limits to 150,000 words
  • Subscription plans can be a bit pricey 
  • Plagiarism checker is only available in a premium plan
  • Doesn’t offer a free trial
  • No refund policy
  • The free version is ideal for basic spelling and grammatical mistakes, but it does not correct advanced writing issues.
  • Some features are not available for Mac.

ProwritingAid Pros

  • It offers more than 20 different reports to help you improve your writing.
  • Less expensive than other grammar checkers.
  • This tool helps you strengthen your writing style as it offers big-picture feedback.
  • ProWritingAid has a life plan with no further payments required.
  • Compatible with Google Docs!
  • Prowritingaid works on both Windows and Mac.
  • They offer more integrations than most tools.

ProWritingAid Cons

  • Editing can be a little more time-consuming when you add larger passages of text.
  • ProWritingAid currently offers no mobile app for Android or iOS devices.
  • Plagiarism checker is only available in premium plans.
  • All recommendations are not accurate

Summarizing the Ginger VS Grammarly: My Recommendation

As both writing assistants are great in their own way, you need to choose the one that suits you best.

  • For example, go for Grammarly  if you are a non-fiction writer
  • Go for ProWritingAid if you are a fiction writer.
  • ProWritingAid is better at catching errors found in long-form content. However, Grammarly is more suited to short blog posts and other similar tasks.
  • ProWritingAid helps you clean up your writing by checking for style, structure, and content while Grammarly focuses on grammar and punctuation.
  • Grammarly has a more friendly UI/UX whereas; ProWritingAid offers complete feedback on big picture writing.

Both ProWritingAid and Grammarly are awesome writing tools, without a doubt. but as per my experience, Grammarly is a winner here because Grammarly helps you to review and edit your content. Grammarly highlights all the mistakes in your writing within seconds of copying and pasting the content into Grammarly’s editor or using the software’s native feature in other text editors.

Not only does it identify tiny grammatical and spelling errors, it tells you when you overlook punctuations where they are needed. And, beyond its plagiarism-checking capabilities, Grammarly helps you proofread your content. Even better, the software offers a free plan that gives you access to some of its features.

#9604. Ollama /api/embed Silently Dropped 45% of My Document

Posted on Nov 15 • Originally published at Medium

On a machine without a GPU, Ollama 0.40.14 loaded qwen3-embedding:0.6b with a 4,096-token context, and /api/embed cut my 7,510-token document down to 4,095 tokens with no error, no warning and no flag in the response. Send "truncate": false so an overlong input fails with HTTP 400, and split documents into chunks of about 2,000 characters before you embed them.

This story was written with the assistance of an AI writing program. Every number below comes from one run on an 8-core Linux box with no GPU: Ollama 0.40.14, qwen3-embedding:0.6b (Q8_0, 1,024 dimensions) and Python 3.14.4 calling the HTTP API with urllib. The test document is the GPL-3 license text (35,149 characters).

/api/show reports qwen3.context_length = 32768 for this model. That is what the model was trained for, not what the server used. After the first request, /api/ps listed the loaded model with context_length=4096, and the server log said why: msg="vram-based default context" total_vram="0 B" default_num_ctx=4096.

With no VRAM to measure, the server picked 4,096 tokens. Embedding requests run in that same context, so one embedding sees at most 4,095 tokens of input.

I wrote one fact that appears nowhere in the license: "The staging cluster's nightly backup runs at 02:30 UTC and keeps 14 snapshots." Then I embedded three documents: the license alone, the license with the fact appended at the end, and the license with the fact at the start. The query was "When does the staging cluster's nightly backup run?"

The vector for "license plus fact at the end" is identical to the vector for the license alone: all 1,024 floats equal. Both score 0.2773 against the query. Put the same sentence first and the score jumps to 0.7830. In a RAG index this is the quiet kind of failure: the chunk is stored, the vector looks normal, and nothing in the second half of the text can ever be retrieved.

The response has five keys, and none of them is a truncation flag. The only hint is prompt_eval_count = 4095, the context minus one, and you only notice it if you compare it with what you sent. The runner's log line for the same request reads n_tokens = 4095, truncated = 0, so grepping the server log for truncation finds nothing either.

The behaviour is documented. The API reference says truncate "truncates the end of each input to fit within context length. Returns error if false and context length is exceeded. Defaults to true". The default is the trap. At this text's 4.7 characters per token, everything after roughly the first 19,000 characters was dropped.

This is the guard I now put in front of every embedding call:

A short input still returns a 1,024-dimension vector. The full license raised HTTPError 400 after 0.03 seconds with {"error":"the input length exceeds the context length"}. That is the failure you want: fast, loud, and before a useless vector lands in the index. The silent version took 44.6 seconds to produce that useless vector.

The fix that worked was splitting the text on paragraph boundaries into chunks of at most 2,000 characters. That gave 20 chunks, the longest 1,992 characters, sent as one batch with truncate: false. The batch returned HTTP 200 in 54.1 seconds for 7,529 tokens. The chunk holding the fact ranked first of 20 with a cosine of 0.8372; the next best scored 0.3272.

The other obvious fix is a bigger context. I started a second server with OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH=16384 and embedded the whole document in one call. All 7,510 tokens were read this time, and the fact did move the vector: the query scored 0.6103 against the license with the fact and 0.3650 without it. That is retrievable, but far weaker than 0.8372, because one vector now has to summarise 7,500 tokens of license text plus one sentence about backups.

The single 7,510-token embedding took 124.0 seconds. The 20 chunks covering the same text took 54.1 seconds, 2.3 times faster. The loaded model grew too: /api/ps reported 1.24 GB at a 4,096-token context, 1.72 GB at 8,192 and 2.70 GB at 16,384. A per-request "options": {"num_ctx": 8192} also raised the context, but the server reloaded the model to apply it, so mixing context sizes across requests means reloads.

I did not test a GPU machine; its default context may be larger, but the trap is the same whenever a document is longer than the loaded context.
