#9590. Crypto: Balancing Potential and Limitations – What Problems Can Digital Currencies Actually Solve?

The most enthusiastic crypto supporters once claimed (and some still do) that digital currencies can address all the flaws, risks, gaps, and shortcomings that burden the traditional financial system and that so many people are dissatisfied with. Except the reality has demonstrated they quite obviously can’t.

Crypto is indeed an exciting and promising innovation that has already proven it can be useful in many real-life situations, but that doesn’t automatically turn it into a fix-it-all. It’s not able to substitute fiat, nor can it single-handedly address issues like economic inequalities, structural inflation, security risks, and other similar problems.

However, if crypto were completely useless, we wouldn’t still be talking or hearing about it so often – but we are. If you want to know how far digital currencies have come and what’s happening in the crypto space at the moment, you can check out the Top Cryptocurrency News Today | Binance Square and read about the latest events and developments in the industry.

So, if crypto can’t bring world peace, what exactly can it do, and how far do its powers extend?

People were initially reluctant to engage with crypto and didn’t know what to make of it, but once the fear of the unknown subsided and curiosity took over, they realized that digital currencies possess certain qualities that can make them useful in various circumstances, as follows.

Diversification is a must in investment in order to reduce the risk of losses, and it relies on a simple principle of spreading capital across various types of assets with different risk profiles instead of concentrating it in a single one. Over the years, crypto has grown into quite a popular investment tool, even though it was intended to serve as a payment solution. Long story short, digital currencies have found their way into many investors’ holdings, and some of them have earned substantial profits from their crypto investments.

A portfolio can be well-balanced even if it doesn’t contain a single crypto, so digital assets aren’t a requirement for diversification. But the fact that they have a relatively low correlation to traditional markets, being driven by a different combination of factors, and can bring in outsized gains due to their sharp price swings makes them a good choice in this respect. Nevertheless, experts recommend keeping crypto allocations low (between 1% and 5% of a total portfolio) to protect against volatility risks.

Crypto is powered by blockchain technology, which means issuance and transactions are managed by a network of nodes instead of a single central entity, like governments, banks, and payment processors. This unique structure gives crypto the possibility to help with economic mobility.

By removing the intermediaries, coins can be transferred directly from one person to another, so the funds can arrive in the recipient’s wallet almost instantly, whereas with fiat, it can take up to several days for transactions to be processed, especially for international transfers that involve more cumbersome bureaucratic procedures.

Transaction speed is not the only aspect that crypto can improve, but affordability as well. Because there are no middlemen to incur processing fees, transferring crypto is cheaper than transferring conventional currencies.

And let’s not forget about all the people in the world who can’t use banking services because of all the barriers they impose. Crypto is easily accessible to everyone as long as they have a smart device and internet connection.

Another advantage that derives from crypto’s decentralized architecture is the ability to conceal users’ real identity. Crypto wallets are pseudonymous, so holders are not required to share sensitive data like legal names and personal addresses in order to use crypto. The blockchain also offers a public record of all the transactions it has ever processed, giving everyone the possibility to verify transfers and offering a level of transparency that fiat money cannot match.

The advantages that crypto offers seem absolutely amazing, but volatility casts a shadow over all these perks. Digital currencies can be a good addition to investors’ holdings, as they can offer high growth, but if the allocations are not well balanced, a market downturn can drag the entire portfolio down.

At the same time, the alleged decentralization that removes intermediaries from the equation and makes crypto transactions faster and cheaper in theory doesn’t always apply in practice. In many situations, crypto transactions run through centralized exchanges, or the projects are controlled by a foundation or corporate entity, which goes against the decentralization ethos that digital assets promote. So, instead of offering a different path to transferring value than traditional finance, crypto often uses the same centralized mechanism.

Using crypto to pay for goods and services is not practical because, once again, volatility gets in the way. With crypto values shifting constantly, it’s extremely challenging for companies that accept crypto payments to price their products and protect their profits. Many resort to payment processors to help them deal with volatility, but that kind of contradicts the whole idea of embracing crypto to bypass the middlemen.

It’s bold, if not downright absurd, to say that crypto can provide the answer to all of society’s money-related problems. But it’s equally absurd to dismiss it as a useless tool when it’s already being used in so many areas, and its integration into global finance continues to grow. Digital currencies can step in instances and areas where conventional banking services are either absent or highly inefficient. The takeaway here is that they can only serve as a complementary solution, not a complete replacement for traditional financial systems.

#9589. Bubble Sort Explained with Simple Python Examples

Posted on Nov 15 • Originally published at codingcush.com

Bubble sort is a simple sorting algorithm that compares neighbouring items again and again and swaps them whenever they are in the wrong order. After each full pass, the biggest unsorted value has bubbled up to its correct place at the end. In this guide you will dry run bubble sort on a small list, write the basic Python version, improve it with a swapped flag, count its comparisons and swaps, and see how it compares with Python's built in sorted(). Every output comes from running this article's code on Python 3.12.3.

Imagine students lined up by height, but shuffled. You walk along the line looking at each pair of neighbours. Whenever the taller student stands in front of the shorter one, they swap. By the end of the walk, the tallest student is at the back, having won every swap.

That walk is called a pass. On the next pass, the second tallest ends up just before the tallest. Pass by pass, the sorted part grows at the end. The algorithm stops when a pass finishes with no swaps, which means everything is in order.

Two details matter. Bubble sort only compares neighbours, never distant items. And equal values never swap, because we swap only when the left value is strictly greater. That makes it stable: equal items keep their original relative order.

Let us sort [5, 2, 9, 1, 5, 6] by hand. In pass 1 we swap 5 and 2, keep 5 before 9, then swap 9 past 1, 5 and 6:

Pass 2 pushes the 1 forward. Pass 3 swaps 2 and 1, and the list is sorted. Pass 4 changes nothing, and that quiet pass proves we can stop. After each pass, one more position at the end is final, so the unsorted part shrinks by one item every time.

Here is the plain version. It copies the input first, so the caller's list is never changed:

The outer loop runs the passes. The inner loop walks the still unsorted part, which is why its range is n - 1 - i: after i passes, the last i items are sorted and need no more checks. The swap line exchanges two neighbours in one step, with no temporary variable. Python builds the right hand pair first, then unpacks it, so nothing is overwritten early.

Adding two counters to the same code gave this real result on our test list:

Fifteen comparisons for six items is no coincidence. The passes compare 5, then 4, then 3, then 2, then 1 pairs, which sums to 15. Double the list and the comparisons roughly quadruple. That is the whole complexity story in one sentence.

A terminal window showing the real bubble sort run tested for this article: pass by pass states, comparison and swap counts, the early stop on sorted input, and the timing test against sorted().

The basic version keeps passing even when the list became sorted early. The fix is a flag named swapped: False at the start of each pass, True on any swap, and stop if a full pass ends with it still False. The shrinking range stays:

Running this version on the already sorted list [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6] gave:

One pass, five comparisons, done. On our shuffled test list the same code needed 4 passes and 14 comparisons, one fewer than the basic version, because it skipped the pointless final pass. A small win here, but a huge win on nearly sorted input.

For n items, bubble sort makes about n passes of up to n comparisons, so the work grows with n squared: O(n^2) on average and in the worst case. The best case belongs to the optimised version on sorted input, where one pass of n comparisons proves the job is done: O(n). Extra memory is O(1), because sorting happens in place. If Big O itself feels fuzzy, our guide to Big O notation explained simply, with everyday examples builds the idea from scratch.

In real Python code you would rarely ship bubble sort, because sorted() returns a new sorted list in one line:

The official Python sorting guide explains that sorted() uses Timsort, which spots runs of already ordered data and merges them, making it fast and stable. The built in functions documentation covers sorted() itself, including its key and reverse options. We timed both on the same 1,000 random numbers (seed 42):

Exact timings vary by machine, but the gap widens as lists grow, because O(n log n) pulls away from O(n^2) quickly.

Bubble sort is useful for learning how sorting, loops and complexity fit together, for interviews about swaps, and for tiny, nearly sorted lists, where the optimised version finishes in a pass or two.

It is not useful for large data or production Python code. If your list has thousands of items and you wrote two nested loops, the honest fix is not a cleverer bubble sort. It is sorted(). The neighbour thinking still pays off elsewhere, for example when you compare a stack vs a queue and how each one orders its items.

Off by one in the inner range. Writing range(n - i) instead of range(n - 1 - i) lets j reach the last index, and a[j + 1] raises IndexError: list index out of range. The minus 1 exists because the loop looks one step ahead.

Resetting the swapped flag in the wrong place. If swapped = False sits inside the inner loop, the flag forgets earlier swaps and the sort can stop early. The reset belongs at the start of each pass.

Sorting the caller's list by accident. If the caller still needs the original order, copy first with numbers[:], or use sorted(), which returns a new list.

Because the largest unsorted value rises to the end on every pass, the way a bubble rises through water.

Yes, in the form shown here. We swap only when the left value is strictly greater, so equal items never change their relative order.

Almost never. Use sorted() or the list sort() method: faster, tested and shorter. Bubble sort earns its place in learning and interviews.

Selection sort and insertion sort come next, then merge sort. After that, recursion explained with simple Python examples unlocks the divide and conquer sorts, built on a function that calls itself.

Bubble sort does one humble thing well: it teaches you to watch an algorithm work. You saw [5, 2, 9, 1, 5, 6] settle into order, counted its 15 comparisons and 6 swaps, watched the optimised version quit after one pass on sorted input, and measured sorted() finishing about 305 times faster on 1,000 items. Learn it for the thinking, then sort real lists the Python way.

#9588. Taco Bell Made An Exclusive Hot Dog & Fans Are Freaking Out

“Imagine getting a glizzy from Taco Bell 😭”

Taco Bell is no stranger to controversial menu items, but one new viral dish might be the wildest yet.

Last week, the Tex-Mex chain launched the first-ever Live Más Open, a star-studded golf tournament hosted by Kevin Hart. The guest list for the nine-hole competition included pro athletes, television stars, musicians, and more. However, the appearance that’s generating the most buzz isn’t a celebrity—it’s a Taco Bell hot dog.

Attendees were served a lineup of event-exclusive dishes that we've never seen at the Bell before, like lemon pepper ranch-dusted chicken nuggets and pimento cheese Quesaritos. Taco Bell fans, though, have the most FOMO for the Clubhouse Street Dog.

According to Taco Bell, the dish featured an all-beef hot dog served in a puffy flatbread instead of a traditional bun. Taco Bell loaded the hot dog with charred pineapple, cotija, citrus-pickled red onions, and cilantro. The whole thing is drizzled with a Fire Piña Aioli and sour cream.

Bailey Fink from Allrecipes attended the Live Más Open and tasted the hot dog for herself. She called it “easily one of the best hot dogs I’ve ever had” from a fast-food restaurant and compared the flavor profile to a traditional Colombian hot dog (minus the potato chips).

Social media users who didn't get the chance to try the Clubhouse Street Dog, though, don't seem too convinced. “The words Taco Bell and hot dog should not be in the same sentence,” one Instagram user wrote. Another added, “If you order a hot dog from Taco Bell, you need to be on watch list…”

But if you take a look at Taco Bell's origin story, introducing hot dogs would actually bring the chain full circle. Founder Glen Bell's early restaurants served hamburgers and hot dogs before he shifted his attention to tacos. He eventually opened Taco Tia, which preceded the first Taco Bell restaurant in Downey, California.

Unfortunately, though, it appears Taco Bell won't be adding hot dogs to the menu anytime soon. “The Live Más Open menu was created exclusively for the tournament day, allowing us to showcase our Taco Bell twist on classic golf bites,” a Taco Bell representative tells Delish. “There are no current plans to bring the menu nationwide, but at Taco Bell, we never say never.”

But don't despair: Part of the golf tournament prize is the opportunity to help choose a discontinued menu item to bring back for a limited time next year. So while a Taco Bell hot dog likely isn't in our immediate future, we can still look forward to the return of an old favorite.

#9585. I Tried Keurig’s First-Ever Espresso Machine—Is It Worth Adding To Your Coffee Routine?

I’ve owned a Keurig, I’ve owned a Nespresso, and I’ve spent way too much money on coffee shop runs in between. Needless to say, I’m an expert on the subject. So when I heard that Keurig was launching its first-ever espresso machine, my interest was piqued. Could the brand that turned single-serve coffee into the household standard successfully switch up its game?

Keurig’s latest and possibly greatest innovation—a two-in-one single-serve coffee maker and espresso machine called the Alta System—will turn your home kitchen into a coffee shop thanks to a multifunctional design that brews everything from regular coffee to espresso, cappuccinos, and lattes. It comes with a built-in milk frother and functions exclusively on the new plastic- and aluminum-free pods (sustainability, hallelujah!).

Here’s whether the Keurig Alta System lives up to the hype, how it compares to other machines, and whether it deserves a spot on your own kitchen coffee bar.

Let’s go a little more in-depth, shall we? The Keurig Alta System is the brand’s new single-serve coffee and espresso machine that does a lot more than your standard K-Cup brewer. Unlike the brand’s traditional lineup, which uses K-Cup pods, the Alta introduces an entirely new innovation: AltaRounds. Your machine can read a code on the AltaRounds and adjust its brew settings accordingly, whether that’s pressure, temperature, or the water-to-coffee ratio. (K-Cups are still compatible with the Alta).

The integrated milk frother is another major upgrade for Keurig, letting you make hot and cold foam.

The Keurig Alta System is $499.99, which, yes, is pricier than other Keurig models. However, classic espresso machines can run you upwards of $1,000.

As for the AltaRounds, they’re sold in boxes of eight, ranging from $9.99 to $10.99 depending on the variety. If you wanna break that up by coffee, it’s about $1.25 to $1.37 a cup. Not too shabby.

As someone who is impatient and terrible at reading directions (hello, your type B friend reporting for duty), I wasn’t overly optimistic I’d figure it out that quickly. But it’s actually an easy device to navigate, thanks to the convenient LED screen that walks you through the whole process.

I was immediately transfixed by the machine. I texted my boyfriend, “I’m in love with it,” before it even finished brewing my first coffee. The Alta feels so much chicer on my countertops, and the pods are smaller and store more easily. Once I finally took that first sip, I was ready to toss my old Keurig in the trash (respectfully).

The drip coffee and espresso shots taste like something straight from an award-winning barista. I love the flexibility to make a black coffee one day and an iced caramel latte the next. And the milk frother just takes the entire thing to the next level.

Listen, $500 for a coffee machine is a lot. And maybe because of that, this isn’t an upgrade you can make immediately. Still, the Keurig Alta System is worth the hype; if you can swap your classic single-serve maker for it, you should. It checks literally every box—it’s more aesthetic, more versatile, and more sustainable.

The only caveat is if you’re the type of person who exclusively drinks drip coffee. In that case, it might not be worth the splurge. But if you want to cosplay as a barista and whip up new creations, from frothy cappuccinos to iced lattes and espresso martinis, the Alta provides all the room to experiment (and it will ultimately save you money on those $10 coffee runs).

#9583. Is a gas oven bad for bread?: Why a gas oven may be interfering with your go-to steaming method.

Adapted from King Arthur Baking Company’s Big Book of Bread

One of the most crucial steps for making crusty artisan-style bread comes at the very end: steaming.

Baking bread with steam is critical for achieving expansive, open-crumbed loaves with a golden, crisp crust. If you bake bread in a dry oven, the crust quickly sets, which prevents the dough from expanding to its full potential; this, in turn, leads to loaves with a denser crumb. If you introduce steam at the start of the bake, the crust remains moist and pliable and the loaf can stretch and expand before the crust sets, resulting in a lighter, more open crumb.

What’s more, steam also helps gelatinize starches on the loaf’s exterior, which helps it brown and creates an especially crispy, flavorful, and shiny loaf. (Learn more: A guide to baking bread with steam at home.)

There are many different ways to steam your bread, all of which are designed to introduce moisture to the oven during the first part of baking. The most common method involves setting a large cast-iron skillet below your baking stone or steel when you preheat the oven. After you load your bread into the oven, you immediately pour a cup or so of warm water into the preheated cast-iron skillet and quickly close the door so the steam doesn’t escape.

This method works great, with one exception: It’s not effective in a gas oven.

If you have a gas oven, it’s very hard to add sufficient steam. By design, gas ovens vent out effluence, meaning whatever steam you add is very quickly vented out of the oven chamber. This is particularly true if you steam your bread by pouring hot water into a cast-iron skillet, as outlined above. All the water quickly dissipates, and there’s not enough moisture left to enhance the crust.

But all is not lost. There is a workaround.

If you’re steaming bread in a gas oven, you need to use a preheated covered baker, such as a Dutch oven. Instead of adding an additional water source, the lidded vessel traps the steam that escapes from the loaf as it bakes, becoming a kind of self-steaming oven. Because the steam is sealed in, the gas oven won’t vent it out.

You can use a Dutch oven for a round, boule-shaped loaf, or any other form of covered baker, like the Brod & Taylor Bread Steel for elongated, bâtard-shaped loaves. (There’s also a round version of the Bread Steel available.)

For more guidance on this method, see our previous blogs, Bread baking in a Dutch oven and For crispy, crackle crusts, put a lid on it.

When you load your dough into the oven, slip a few ice cubes between the parchment beneath your loaf and the pan to give the loaf an extra initial burst of steam. Just don’t skip the parchment beneath the dough. Otherwise, the extra water from the melting ice may cause your bread to stick to the pot.

#9581. Popular Thanksgiving Product Recalled From Costco Shelves Over Concerning Contamination Risk

Here's what shoppers need to know ahead of the holiday.

Delish editors handpick every product we feature. We may earn commission from the links on this page.

Costco members, listen up. A popular Thanksgiving topping is being recalled over concerns about possible cleaning chemical contamination. Here's what to watch for.

Costco is recalling its Kirkland Signature Real Heavy Whipped Cream ahead of the upcoming Thanksgiving holiday. The recall covers 15-ounce cans sold between October 11 and October 31, 2026, including those purchased in three-packs.

To identify the affected product, check for item number 1777000, item code AC50, and a best-if-used-by date of April 2, 2027. The cans must also have a printed timestamp between 00:35 and 02:45.

The whipped cream was sold at Costco warehouses in 12 states: Alabama, Florida, Georgia, Iowa, Illinois, Indiana, Missouri, Mississippi, North Carolina, South Carolina, Tennessee, and Wisconsin.

Producer Alamance Foods voluntarily recalled the product after learning that one batch may contain a small amount of a cleaning chemical. According to a November 7 letter sent to Costco members, some shoppers reported a chemical smell and taste.

The company said no serious adverse health effects requiring medical care had been reported. The notice does not identify the chemical or say how it may have gotten into the whipped cream.

If your can matches the affected lot and timestamp, stop using it and return it to your local Costco for a full refund. The company's notice also includes photographs of the can and its printed code to help shoppers identify the product.

For questions or concerns, contact Alamance Foods at customer.care@alamancefood.com.

#9577. 3 Easy Hacks To Make Instant Mashed Potatoes WAY Better

You might prefer homemade mashed potatoes, but sometimes you just need a shortcut—and on days like that, grabbing the box is WAY easier. But while the back-of-the-box directions will yield just-fine results, a few easy hacks will give you much better results.

As a recipe developer and professional cook, I don’t often make instant mashed potatoes, but I was excited by the challenge of leveling them up—without adding a bunch of extra ingredients or steps that take the convenience out of this convenience food. So I tried making instant mashed potatoes every way I could think of (including the way the box says!). In the end, I found three tricks that, while super simple, massively improve that final bowl of mashed potatoes.

Here are three ways to instantly upgrade instant mashed potatoes.

Most boxes tell you to rehydrate instant mashed potato flakes in hot water enriched with a little butter and a few tablespoons of milk—but I’m going all in on the milk here. The extra dairy really fills out the flavor of the mashed potato and makes it creamier—especially if you’re using a higher-fat milk, like whole or 2%.

When swapping milk for water, it’s best to increase the liquid amount just slightly. For some reason (totally scientific, I’m sure!), the potato flakes require more milk than water to hydrate properly. I recommend 2 extra tablespoons for every half cup of instant mashed potatoes.

Also, add the extra milk the box typically calls for. If you leave it out, the potatoes will be dry. When I was testing, I found it didn’t really matter when that second amount of milk went into the pan (at the beginning versus just before the potatoes), but some boxes emphasize putting it in cold just before adding the potatoes—so if you want to do that to make you feel safer, be my guest!

All the instant mashed potatoes I made lacked seasoning—until I doubled the salt. Then they were perfect. Now here’s the thing: I was testing with Diamond Crystal kosher salt, which is less salty by volume than table salt or Morton’s kosher. The back of the instant mashed potato box didn’t specify what type of salt they used, so if they tested with a fine salt or Morton’s kosher, maybe ¼ teaspoon was the perfect amount. But in my kitchen with Diamond Crystal, it was woefully underseasoned.

Maybe you’re nervous about oversalting and don’t want to double or even slightly increase the salt right away. But regardless, I’m begging you: Taste those potatoes before you serve them and don’t feel bad if you have to add another hefty pinch.

You might assume that mashed potatoes should be made in a pot—I definitely did. But the fluffiest, creamiest instant potatoes I made in this whole testing process came from a wide, high-sided sauté pan. The reason for this? Absolute science.

When adding the instant potato flakes to the hot liquid, the goal is to distribute them as evenly as possible without working them too much. Yes, the back of the box says to “stir” the potatoes in, but in testing, I quickly discovered that even a few strokes can quickly lead to gummy potatoes.

Here’s where the pan size comes in. Using a wide pan increases the liquid's surface area, so you can sprinkle the potatoes evenly over the top and pat them down into the liquid instead of stirring. From there, let them stand until they’ve absorbed the liquid, then give them a few stirs. Trust me: They’ll be way fluffier because you messed with them less!

#9572. Cranberry Pie

What People Are Saying:“I made 3 desserts this Thanksgiving and this was an absolute hit!! Everyone at the table raved about it including my super picky 7 year old who had herself seconds. Definitely a winner and will be making again.” - PurplePuzzle

Preheat your oven to 350° and grease a 9-inch pie plate with butter.

For the crust, grab a large bowl and mix together the Biscoff crumbs, melted butter, and a pinch of salt. Gently press this mixture into the bottom and up the sides of your greased pie plate.

Bake the crust until it turns golden and feels firm to the touch. Once done, set it aside on a wire rack to cool.

In a small bowl, mix the gelatin with some cold water and let it sit so it can bloom.

Next, for the filling, grab a medium saucepan, toss in the cranberries, brown sugar, orange juice, and zest, and bring it to a simmer over medium heat. Stir occasionally while the cranberries burst and the liquid has thickened slightly, which should take about 7 minutes.

Pour in the coconut milk, ginger, heavy cream, almond extract, and a little salt. Stir everything together and heat until it’s nice and steamy, but not quite simmering. Remove from the heat and stir in the bloomed gelatin until fully dissolved.

Now, blend the cranberry mixture until it’s super smooth—use whatever blender or food processor you have handy. Strain it into a bowl, toss out any solids, and let the mixture cool down to room temperature. Pour the cranberry filling into your crust and refrigerate until set, which should take at least 6 hours.

Serve with homemade whipped cream and enjoy!

The full list of ingredients and instructions can be found in the recipe below.

This pie will keep for up to a week in the fridge and frozen for up to 5 months. Simply thaw it out in the fridge the next day and serve.

Every November 11, Americans celebrate and thank those who have served in our military. Veterans Day marks the anniversary of the 1918 armistice that ended World War I, but it wasn’t until 1954, after both World War II and the Korean War, that it changed nationally from Armistice Day to Veterans Day.

To mark the occasion, many of our favorite national food chains are dishing out free meals, drinks, and treats to both active-duty military and vets. Here’s where you can score big.

Aroma Joe’s is offering veterans free handcrafted coffee or signature AJ’s Rush Energy Drink in any size up to 24 ounces at all locations with a valid ID.

Veterans and active-duty military members can get 10 free Boneless Wings + Fries with valid proof of service at participating BWW sports bars for dine-in only and GO locations with a minimum $5 purchase.

All active military members and veterans can enjoy a free All-American Single Smash or Americana Big Dog in-restaurant.

All active-duty service members and veterans with proof of service can enjoy a free Red, White, and Blueberry Pancake Combo that includes two buttermilk pancakes topped with glazed strawberries, blueberry topping, and whipped topping, along with two eggs, hash browns, and a choice of two strips of hickory-smoked bacon or two pork sausage links.

Active and retired military members can receive a free Original French Toast during operating hours for dine-in orders.

Active-duty, retired military members, and veterans can enjoy a complimentary order of Bang Bang Shrimp and a nonalcoholic beverage when dining at any Bonefish Grill location.

All active and retired military can enjoy a free donut.

All active military and veterans can receive a free single ShackBurger with a valid military ID or proof of service.

All active-duty and retired military members can enjoy a free meal from the chain’s special Veterans Day menu, with the purchase of a beverage when dining in at participating locations. The menu includes the option of 10-Piece Original Wings, Cheeseburger, Buffalo Chicken Sandwich, or Chicken Caesar Salad.

The bagel chain is offering veterans and active military a free coffee and bagel with schmear all day long. The offer includes any size hot or iced coffee and any bagel with any schmear and is only available in the bakery.

Gold Star Families, active military, veterans, and first responders can get a complimentary 5-Course Teppanyaki Entree, including a choice of Hibachi Steak, Chicken, or Salmon. The offer is available for dine-in only and requires the purchase of an appetizer or starter.

Veterans and military members can order a free Spaghetti with Marinara or Meat Sauce with proof of veteran or military status by using the code VET26.

All current and retired military members can enjoy a complimentary buffet and beverage at Golden Corral locations nationwide.

Active-duty military and veterans can enjoy a complimentary choice of 10 Bone-In or Boneless Wings, Beer-Battered Fish & Chips, Steakburger, Chicken Caesar Salad, Buttermilk Crispy Chicken Sandwich, or Chicken BLT Tacos.

Veterans and active military personnel can enjoy a free small hot or iced coffee and a free donut of their choice.

#9566. Top 10 AI Tools in 2023 That Will Make Your Life Easier



 In this article, we explore the top 10 AI tools that are driving innovation and efficiency in various industries. These tools are designed to automate repetitive tasks, improve workflow, and increase productivity. The tools included in our list are some of the most advanced and widely used in the market, and are suitable for a variety of applications. Some of the tools focus on natural language processing, such as ChatGPT and Grammarly, while others focus on image and video generation, such as DALL-E and Lumen5. Other tools such as OpenAI Codex, Tabnine, Canva, Jasper AI,, and Surfer SEO are designed to help with specific tasks such as code understanding content writing and website optimization. This list is a great starting point for anyone looking to explore the possibilities of AI and how it can be applied to their business or project.

So let’s dive into

1. ChatGPT

ChatGPT is a large language model that generates human-like responses to a variety of prompts. It can be used for tasks such as language translation, question answering, and text completion. It can handle a wide range of topics and styles of writing, and generates coherent and fluent text, but should be used with care as it may generate text that is biased, offensive, or factually incorrect.

Pros:

  • Generates human-like responses to a variety of prompts
  • Can be fine-tuned for specific tasks such as language translation, question answering, and text completion
  • Can handle a wide range of topics and styles of writing
  • Can generate coherent and fluent text, even when completing a given text prompt.

Cons:

  • May generate text that is biased or offensive
  • Can generate text that is not accurate or factually correct
  • May require large amounts of computational resources to run
  • The model can sometimes generate text that is not coherent or fluent, depending on the prompt given.

Overall, ChatGPT is a powerful tool for natural language processing, but it should be used with care and with an understanding of its limitations.

2. DALL-E

DALL-E is a generative model developed by OpenAI that is capable of generating images from text prompts. It is based on the GPT-3 architecture, which is a transformer-based neural network language model that has been trained on a massive dataset of text. DALL-E can generate images that are similar to a training dataset and it can generate high-resolution images that are suitable for commercial use.

Pros:

  • Generates high-resolution images
  • Can generate images from text prompts
  • It can be fine-tuned for specific tasks such as generating images of a certain style or category

Cons:

  • May generate images that are not entirely original and could be influenced by the training data
  • May require significant computational resources to run
  • The quality of the generated images may vary depending on the specific prompt

Overall, DALL-E is a powerful AI-based tool for generating images, it can be used for a variety of applications such as creating images for commercial use, gaming, and other creative projects. It is important to note that the generated images should be reviewed and used with care, as they may not be entirely original and could be influenced by the training data.

3. Lumen5

Lumen5 is a content creation platform that uses AI to help users create videos, social media posts, and other types of content. It has several features that make it useful for content creation and marketing, including:

Pros:

  • Automatically summarizes text from a blog post, article, or another source into a script for a video or social media post
  • Offers a library of royalty-free videos, images, and music to use in content
  • Has a drag-and-drop interface for easy content creation
  • Can create videos in multiple languages
  • Has a built-in analytics tool to track the performance of created content.

Cons:

  • The quality of the generated content may vary depending on the source material
  • The automatic summarization feature may not always capture the main points of the source material
  • The library of videos, images, and music is limited.
  • The analytics feature is basic

Overall, Lumen5 is a useful tool for creating content quickly and easily, it can help automate the process of creating videos, social media posts, and other types of content. However, the quality of the generated content may vary depending on the source material and it is important to review and edit the content before publishing it.

4. Grammarly

Grammarly is a writing-enhancement platform that uses AI to check for grammar, punctuation, and spelling errors in the text. It also provides suggestions for improving the clarity, concision, and readability of the text. It has several features that make it useful for improving writing, including:

Pros:

  • Checks for grammar, punctuation, and spelling errors in the text
  • Provides suggestions for improving clarity, concision, and readability
  • Can be integrated with various apps and platforms such as Microsoft Office, Google Docs, and social media platforms
  • Offers a browser extension and a desktop app
  • Has a premium version with more advanced features such as plagiarism detection and more

Cons:

  • The suggestions provided may not always be accurate or appropriate
  • The grammar checker may not always recognize context-specific language use
  • The free version has limited features
  • Limited to English language only
  • Overall, Grammarly is a useful tool for improving writing, it can help users identify and correct grammar and punctuation errors, and improve the clarity, concision, and readability of their text. However, it is important to review the suggestions provided by the tool and use them with caution, as they may not always be accurate or appropriate.

5.OpenAI Codex

OpenAI Codex is a system developed by OpenAI that can create code from natural language descriptions of software tasks. The system is based on the GPT-3 model and can generate code in multiple programming languages.

Pros:

  • Can automate the process of writing code
  • Can help developers to be more productive
  • Can help non-technical people to create software
  • Can generate code in multiple programming languages

Cons:

  • The quality of the generated code may vary depending on the task description
  • The generated code may not always be optimal or efficient
  • The system may not be able to handle complex software tasks
  • Dependence on the tool may lead to a lack of understanding of the code.

Overall, OpenAI Codex is a powerful tool that can help automate the process of writing code and make it more accessible to non-technical people. However, the quality of the generated code may vary depending on the task description and it is important to review and test the code before using it in a production environment. It is important to use the tool as an aid, not a replacement for the developer's knowledge.

6. Tabnine

Tabnine is a code completion tool that uses AI to predict and suggest code snippets. It is compatible with multiple programming languages and can be integrated with various code editors.

Pros:

  • Can improve coding efficiency by suggesting code snippets based on context
  • Can complete entire code blocks
  • Can predict variables, functions, and other elements of code
  • Can be integrated with various code editors

Cons:

  • The suggestions may not always be accurate or appropriate
  • The system may not always be able to understand the context of the code
  • May not work with all code editors
  • Dependence on the tool may lead to a lack of understanding of the code.

Overall, TabNine is a useful tool for developers that can help improve coding efficiency and reduce the time spent on writing code. However, it is important to review the suggestions provided by the tool and use them with caution, as they may not always be accurate or appropriate. It is important to use the tool as an aid, not a replacement for the developer's knowledge.

7. Jasper AI

Jasper is a content writing and content generation tool that uses artificial intelligence to identify the best words and sentences for your writing style and medium in the most efficient, quick, and accessible way.

Pros:

  • User-friendly interface
  • Generates a wide variety of content types
  • Guarantees 100% unique and free-plagiarism content
  • SEO friendly
  •  Create articles of up to 10k words

Cons:

  • Not the cheapest AI writer on the market

8. Surfer SEO

Surfer SEO is a software tool designed to help website owners and digital marketers improve their search engine optimization (SEO) efforts. The tool provides a variety of features that can be used to analyze a website's on-page SEO, including:

Features:

  • A site audit tool that checks for technical SEO issues
  • A content editor that suggests optimizations for individual pages
  • A keyword research tool that suggests keywords to target
  • A SERP analyzer that shows how a website's pages rank for specific keywords
  • A backlink analysis tool that shows the backlinks pointing to a website.

Pros:

  • Can help website owners and marketers identify technical SEO issues
  • Can provide suggestions for optimizing individual pages
  • Can help with keyword research
  • Can show how a website's pages rank for specific keywords
  • Can provide insight into a website's backlink profile

Cons:

  • Some features may require a paid subscription
  • The tool is not a guarantee of better ranking
  • The tool can only analyze the data it has access to
  • The tool's suggestions may not always be applicable or optimal

Overall, Surfer SEO can be a useful tool for website owners and digital marketers looking to improve their SEO efforts. However, it is important to remember that it is just a tool and should be used in conjunction with other SEO best practices. Additionally, the tool is not a guarantee of better ranking.

9. Zapier

Zapier is a web automation tool that allows users to automate repetitive tasks by connecting different web applications together. It does this by creating "Zaps" that automatically move data between apps, and can also be used to trigger certain actions in one app based on events in another app.

Features:

  • Can connect over 3,000 web applications
  • Can automate repetitive tasks
  • Can create "Zaps" to move data between apps
  • Can trigger certain actions in one app based on events in another app.

Pros:

  • Can automate repetitive tasks
  • Can save time
  • Can improve workflow
  • Can increase productivity
  • Can be integrated with a wide range of web applications

Cons:

  • Can be difficult to set up
  • May require some technical skills
  • May require a paid subscription for some features
  • Some apps may not be compatible
  • Dependence on the tool may lead to a lack of understanding of the apps

Overall, Zapier is a useful tool that can help users automate repetitive tasks and improve workflow. It can save time and increase productivity by connecting different web applications together. However, it may require some technical skills and some features may require a paid subscription. It is important to use the tool with caution and not to rely too much on it, to understand the apps better.

10. Compose AI

Compose AI is a company that specializes in developing natural language generation (NLG) software. Their software uses AI to automatically generate written or spoken text from structured data, such as spreadsheets, databases, or APIs.

Features:

  • Automatically generates written or spoken text from structured data
  • Can be integrated with a wide range of data sources
  • Can be used for a variety of applications such as creating reports, summaries, and explanations
  • Provides an API and a user-friendly interface

Pros:

  • Can automate the process of creating written or spoken content
  • Can help users create more accurate and consistent content
  • Can help users save time by automating repetitive tasks
  • Can be integrated with a wide range of data sources

Cons:

  • The quality of the generated content may vary depending on the data source
  • The generated content may not always be optimal or efficient
  • The system may not be able to handle complex tasks
  • Dependence on the tool may lead to a lack of understanding of the data

Overall, Compose AI's NLG software can be a useful tool for automating the process of creating written or spoken content from structured data. However, the quality of the generated content may vary depending on the data source, and it is essential to review the generated content before using it in a production environment. It is important to use the tool as an aid, not a replacement for the understanding of the data.

Conclusion

AI tools are becoming increasingly important in today's business and technology landscape. They are designed to automate repetitive tasks, improve workflow, and increase productivity. The top 10 AI tools included in this article are some of the most advanced and widely used in the market, and are suitable for various applications. Whether you're looking to improve your natural language processing, create high-resolution images, or optimize your website, there is an AI tool that can help. It's important to research and evaluate the different tools available to determine which one is the best fit for your specific needs. As AI technology continues to evolve, these tools will become even more powerful and versatile and will play an even greater role in shaping the future of business and technology.

#9564. My Local AI Agent Needed a Bigger Brain, So I Gave It a Decentralized GPU

AI Engineer. I ship LLM systems, autonomous agents, and inference pipelines — then write about what I learned

Nosana is an open-source GPU cloud for AI and high-performance workloads, offering lower-cost instant compute.

AI Engineer. I ship LLM systems, autonomous agents, and inference pipelines — then write about what I learned

Nosana is an open-source GPU cloud for AI and high-performance workloads, offering lower-cost instant compute.

AI Engineer. I ship LLM systems, autonomous agents, and inference pipelines — then write about what I learned

Nosana is an open-source GPU cloud for AI and high-performance workloads, offering lower-cost instant compute.

this is my second progress update for the Decentralize AI Hackathon by HackerNoon and Nosana.

In my first article, I Built a Local AI Linux Assistant That Doesn't Rely on the Cloud, I introduced zkzkAgent: an AI agent that manages a Linux machine through plain language and runs entirely on my own hardware with Ollama.

That is still how it works by default. But running everything locally has a ceiling, and I kept hitting it.

To test the integration in real work, I switched to the 27B model on Nosana and gave zkzkAgent a task: create a new project called zkzk_ai, a calculator web app with a FastAPI backend and an HTML, CSS, and JavaScript frontend, and open it in VS Code.

The classifier sent the request to the planner (`NEEDS_PLANNING`). The planner wrote a 9-step plan, including the full content of every file, and then stopped and waited for me:

Once I approved the plan, the executor got to work. It made 10 tool calls, one at a time, across 10 graph iterations (with a maximum of 15).

Wrote static/index.html (2,396 characters)

Wrote static/style.css (1,563 characters)

Wrote static/script.js (2,655 characters)

Nothing complicated happens behind the scenes. The model running on Nosana picks a tool; that tool executes on my machine, and the result is sent back to the model.

To make this clearer, here's an actual example from the execution log (trimmed for readability):Each call follows the same loop. The model on Nosana picks the next tool, the tool runs on my machine, and the result goes back into the conversation. In the log, one turn of that loop looks like this (trimmed):

Next, I asked: "Can you change the zkzk_ai Calculator to be zkzk?" The classifier sent this to the planner as well, which wrote a 7-step plan. After I approved it, the agent read static/index.html and then changed the name in three places: the page title and heading, the FastAPI app title, and the README. It did not touch the calculator logic.

I started the app with `uvicorn app:app`. The page loaded, and the calculator API answered:

Across both requests, every model call in the saved log, 18 in total, went to `inference.nosana.com` and returned `200 OK`. Every file write, command, and app launch happened locally.

I reviewed the code the agent wrote, and tested the backend directly:

- No eval. Expressions are parsed with Python's ast module, and only numbers, parentheses, and `+ - * / // % **` are allowed. When I sent __import__("os"), it was rejected with "Unsupported expression element: Call".

- Clear errors. Division by zero and complex results (such as (-1)**0.5) return a readable message instead of crashing.

- Input limits. Expressions are capped at 500 characters in both the browser and the API.

- Keyboard support. Enter evaluates, Backspace deletes, Esc clears and `^` types a power.

The code is on GitHub at [zkzkGamal/calculator], and the full run log is in the [zkzkAgent repo]

My first article was about an agent that doesn't rely on the cloud. This update doesn't change that. It adds a choice. Private or sensitive work stays on local Ollama, where nothing leaves the machine. Heavy planning can use a much larger model on Nosana's network instead of a centralized provider. In both modes, the tools, the files, and the final yes stay with me.

1. A real benchmark. Run the same five tasks on the local 2B model and on the 27B model on Nosana, and measure success rate, tool calls, time, tokens, and cost. Numbers instead of impressions.

2. Hybrid routing. Because the graph has separate nodes, each node can use its own model. The classifier and chat replies are short and could stay on a small local model, while the planner and executor use Nosana. Plain conversations would then never leave the machine.

3. Automatic fallback. If Nosana can't be reached, switch to local Ollama automatically, the same way the agent already turns Wi-Fi back on by itself.

4. Close the safety gaps. Enforce plan-level confirmations. Also put `run_command` behind a confirmation or an allow-list: today it can run any shell command, and with a remote model choosing the arguments, that matters more than before.

5. Fix the calculator bug with the agent doing the fix.

zkzkAgent: https://github.com/zkzkGamal/zkzkAgent The calculator it built: https://github.com/zkzkGamal/calculator

Full Nosana run log: https://github.com/zkzkGamal/zkzkAgent/blob/main/docs/nosana-run-2026-10-25.log

#9559. We Compared 10 Fast Food Rewards Programs—These Get You A Free Meal The Fastest

I’ve never been more invested in free fries.

I love a good fast food rewards program. There’s something particularly satisfying about opening an app and realizing I’ve accumulated enough points for a free order of fries. But after looking into the rewards programs at some of the country’s biggest chains, I realized that not all points systems are the same.

While restaurants like McDonald’s, Taco Bell, and Wendy’s all let customers earn points toward free food, how much you have to spend before you get something back varies a lot. And just because one restaurant gives you more points per dollar doesn’t necessarily mean you’re getting a better deal.

So I compared the rewards programs at 10 major chains to see how they work, how quickly you can start redeeming points, and what you should know before signing up.

McDonald’s has one of the more straightforward rewards programs. With MyMcDonald’s Rewards, members earn 100 points for every $1 spent on eligible purchases, and rewards start at 1,500 points for smaller items like hash browns or an apple pie.

That means spending just $15 can earn you enough points to start redeeming free food, making it one of the lower entry points among the chains I researched. More substantial menu items like a Big Mac or a Happy Meal cost 7000 points.

The biggest drawback is that points expire on the first day of the month following the sixth month after they’re earned. So if you’re someone who only visits McDonald’s occasionally, you’ll want to make sure those points don’t disappear before you use them.

Burger King’s Royal Perks program awards 10 Crowns for every $1 spent, which customers can redeem for eligible menu items. The lowest tier of redeemable rewards starts at 200 points, so it’ll only take $20 to start receiving freebies like a cheeseburger or a small order of fries. Full meals are available for 1000 points.

The program also comes with a few additional benefits, including opportunities to earn bonus Crowns through challenges and double Crowns during your birthday month.

Like McDonald’s, Burger King generally gives you around six months to redeem your points before they expire. But if you’re regularly ordering Whoppers, those Crowns could add up pretty quickly.

Wendy’s Rewards gives customers 10 points for every $1 spent, and the chain is surprisingly transparent about how many points you’ll need for individual items.

A four-piece order of chicken nuggets costs 200 points, meaning you’ll need to spend $20 to earn enough for that reward. A small order of fries costs 300 points, or $30 in qualifying spending. And you have exactly 365 days to redeem your points before they expire.

For something more substantial, a Baconator requires 900 points, which works out to $90 in spending at the standard earning rate. Personally, I appreciate knowing exactly what I’m working toward, but knowing I’m eating a, technically, $90 Baconator would make me second-guess my choices.

Taco Bell’s rewards program is another relatively simple option, with members earning 10 points for every $1 spent. Once you accumulate 250 points, or the equivalent of $25 in eligible purchases, you’ll unlock a reward from the chain’s available selection. The options range from a medium drink to a crunchy taco.

And if you’re someone who orders Taco Bell regularly, there’s an additional incentive to keep going. Members who earn 2,000 points in a year can reach Fire Tier, increasing their earning rate to 11 points per dollar and unlocking additional reward options. Members have six months to redeem the points before they expire.

Considering how often I find myself in the mood for nachos, this is one program I could see being pretty easy to use.

Chick-fil-A’s rewards program is particularly interesting because the more you spend, the faster you can earn points. New Chick-fil-A One members start at 10 points per dollar, which increases to 11 at Silver status, 12 at Red, and 13 at Signature.

Members can exchange points for eligible food rewards, with the available selection displayed in the app. And, unlike at other chains, Chick-fil-A One points never expire. The first available rewards—like a dessert or a small order of fries—range from 200 to 300 points. A sandwich or eight-count nuggets will cost 800 points, while a full meal is 2500.

The biggest appeal here is that frequent customers can eventually earn more points on the same purchases. However, that also means occasional visitors won’t receive the same earning rate as the chain’s most loyal customers.

Popeyes Rewards also uses a 10-points-per-dollar system, allowing members to exchange accumulated points for eligible menu items. Points expire 180 days after you earn them.

The first tier of rewards unlocks at 300 points, where members can earn a regular drink, a dessert pie, or one of four sides. Full-size entrees are available starting at 600 points.

Popeyes also offers promotional opportunities, including bonus points and special deals, which could make the program more appealing if you’re paying attention to what’s available in the app.

Chipotle Rewards gives customers 10 points for every dollar spent, with points redeemable through its Rewards Exchange for eligible food items. The first available freebies are a side tortilla for 85 points, followed by a bag of chips for 350. You can redeem a full entree for 1625 points.

But what particularly caught my attention was the program’s expiration policy. Unlike chains that automatically expire points after several months, Chipotle lets members keep their balances active by making at least one qualifying purchase per year.

The chain also advertises monthly bonus reward drops and a welcome offer for chips and guacamole with a qualifying purchase. For someone who enjoys Chipotle but doesn’t necessarily order it every week, that flexibility could be a major advantage.

Dunkin’ Rewards is another program that makes earning your first reward relatively accessible. Members receive 10 points for every $1 spent, with redemption options starting at 150 points. That means you can unlock an entry-level reward—like Munchkins, hash browns, and drink add-ons—after $15 in eligible spending.

And if you’re the kind of person who practically lives at Dunkin’, the chain has an additional perk. Members who make 12 qualifying visits in a calendar month can unlock Boosted Status, increasing their earning rate to 12 points per dollar for a limited period.

Dunkin’ also offers triple points on eligible purchases made the day before, on, or the day after your birthday. Points expire 365 days after the last day of the month they were earned.

Panera recently made a major change to its loyalty program, introducing a points-based version of MyPanera in August 2026. The updated system awards 10 points for every $1 spent, with rewards starting at 250 points for a bagel or mini bakery treat. In other words, $25 in eligible purchases can get you started with a free bakery item. Customers who accumulate 2,000 points can redeem them for a full-size entrée.

Panera also offers additional perks, including a welcome points offer, birthday rewards, and special promotions. And once you spend over $300 in qualified purchases within a calendar year, you become eligible for the MyPanera+ tier with even more freebies. Points expire after 180 days of account inactivity.

Starbucks does things a little differently with its Stars system, which received a major update earlier this year. The program now has three membership levels: Green, Gold, and Reserve. Green members earn one Star per dollar spent, while Gold members earn 1.2 Stars and Reserve members earn 1.7 Stars per dollar.

For 25 Stars, you can shave a dollar off drink customizations like extra espresso shots and cold foam. Customers can redeem 60 Stars for $2 off an eligible purchase, while other redemption levels unlock food and drinks. For a new Green member, that means spending $60 at the standard earning rate to unlock the $2 discount, although bonus Star opportunities can help customers get there faster.

Gold and Reserve members also benefit from nonexpiring Stars, giving frequent customers more flexibility when saving up for rewards. Green-tier members must keep their accounts active or forfeit their Stars six months after the month they were earned.

After comparing all 10 programs, one thing became pretty clear: The number of points you earn doesn’t tell the entire story.

McDonald’s and Dunkin’ win for having the lowest reward-redemption thresholds, after $15 in eligible spending. But Popeyes gets points for having the most affordable entrees, which you can redeem after spending $60. Chains like Burger King, Taco Bell, Chipotle, and Panera require $100 or more before you can earn something substantial.

There’s a lot more to consider than just the freebies, though. Chick-fil-A rewards frequent customers with higher earning rates, and Chipotle offers a more forgiving expiration policy.

Personally, I think the best rewards program is the one you’ll actually use. There’s no point spending money at a restaurant you rarely visit just to earn a free item, especially when some points expire before you ever get around to redeeming them.

But if you’re already making regular fast-food runs, signing up for a free rewards program is an easy way to get a little something back. And I’ll never complain about free fries.

#9558. Why Your NumPy Array Changed After Preprocessing (Views vs Copies in ML)

Student focused on web development and programming. I write about debugging, coding challenges, and improving skills.

Student focused on web development and programming. I write about debugging, coding challenges, and improving skills.

Student focused on web development and programming. I write about debugging, coding challenges, and improving skills.

A small NumPy operation can modify data you never intended to touch. Understanding views, copies, and memory sharing can prevent silent bugs in machine learning pipelines.

Imagine preparing a dataset for a machine learning model. You load the original data, select a few columns, normalize their values, and pass the result to your training algorithm.

Later, when you inspect the original dataset, something looks wrong. Some values have changed, even though you never directly modified the original array.

This is one of those Python behaviors that can make debugging surprisingly difficult. The problem usually comes down to how NumPy handles memory. When you create a new array from an existing one, NumPy does not always allocate new memory. Sometimes, it creates a view that points to the same underlying data.

This matters most during preprocessing, where slicing, normalization, reshaping, and feature selection are common. Let’s look at why it happens, how to detect it, and how to avoid it.

A view creates a new array object that shares memory with another array.

A copy creates a separate array with its own data.

The original array changed even though we modified only the view variable. Basic slicing creates a view, so both arrays reference the same memory for the selected elements.

The original array is unchanged. The difference isn’t in the variable names or values. It’s in how NumPy manages memory. If you’ve seen the same idea with plain Python lists, see Why .copy() in Python Still Mutates Your Original List.

Machine learning preprocessing often involves selecting features and transforming numerical values.

Suppose the first two columns are features you want to center around zero. A developer might write:

But the original dataset has also changed:

Slicing created a view of data. Then features -= ... modified the values in place, and since features and data share memory, the change appeared in both.

This is especially dangerous when the original dataset is needed for another preprocessing step, a model comparison, or evaluation.

The processed features are transformed, and the original dataset stays intact.

This .copy() call makes the intent explicit: the preprocessing should work on independent data. Copying everything is not always necessary, though, because it increases memory usage, especially with large datasets. The better habit is knowing when NumPy shares memory and when it doesn’t.

NumPy provides np.shares_memory() for this:

You can also inspect the .base attribute:

The .base attribute shows which array owns the memory behind a view, but it isn’t a complete test for memory sharing. For reliable checks, use np.shares_memory().

A common mistake is assuming that any operation returning a new array creates independent memory. Different operations behave differently:

The key distinction is basic indexing versus advanced indexing.

Basic slicing returns a view, and advanced indexing returns a copy. Two expressions that look like they do the same selection can behave differently in memory, so don’t assume that selecting elements creates independent data.

The difference between in-place and regular arithmetic matters just as much:

In the second version, view + 5 produces a new result, and the name view is rebound to it. The original array is untouched.

Preprocessing code often uses in-place operations to save memory:

If features is a view, the original data changes too.

A typical pipeline includes selecting features, handling missing values, scaling numerical columns, encoding categories, splitting data, and preparing arrays for training. Shared memory can cause trouble at several of these steps.

Problem 1: Accidentally modifying the original dataset. If preprocessing changes the original array, later experiments may use altered values instead of the initial data. Results become hard to reproduce.

Problem 2: Modifying shared training data. If your train and test arrays are views of the same source, an in-place transformation on one can silently change the other. This is a memory-sharing bug, not data leakage, but it can produce results that look valid while being wrong.

Data leakage is a separate issue. It happens when information from the test set influences training, for example by fitting a scaler on the full dataset before splitting. The correct approach is to split first, fit preprocessing only on the training data, and then apply the learned transformation to the test data.

Many scikit-learn transformers, such as StandardScaler, return new arrays by default, so this bug is less common there. Some of them accept a copy=False argument, though, and hand-written in-place NumPy code doesn’t protect you at all.

Problem 3: Difficult debugging. The code runs without errors. The model trains, predictions look reasonable, and metrics seem plausible. The real problem may be hidden in a preprocessing step earlier in the pipeline.

If the original must stay unchanged, make an explicit copy:

Then transform the independent array. For large datasets, weigh the memory cost before copying everything.

NumPy views and copies look similar at first. Both are new variables, both can hold the same values, and both can be passed into machine learning functions. Their memory behavior is different.

A view shares memory with its source, while a copy owns its data. That difference becomes critical when preprocessing uses in-place operations.

The main lesson: don’t assume a new variable means new memory. When a dataset changes unexpectedly, check how the array was created before blaming the preprocessing formula, the model, or the data itself.

Sometimes, the fix is just one missing .copy().

#9556. This fall, reach for this unlikely apple ingredient : Apple cider vinegar is a baker’s secret weapon.

As fall baking season settles in, you're probably reaching for apples — and the many flavor-packed ingredients they produce. Applesauce cooks down into tangy apple butter to be cradled in a flaky galette, while a drop of boiled cider can deliver supercharged apple flavor to crumb cake. But the baking ingredient you may be overlooking may be something you associate more with salad dressings and wellness tonics: apple cider vinegar.

This tangy, apple-y vinegar is a secret ingredient in some of our favorite fall recipes, including cookbook author Claire Saffitz’s Cinnamon-and-Sugar Apple Pie. While lemon juice is the standard acid used in most fruit pie fillings, Claire opts for apple cider vinegar here to complement the filling’s flavors. “It helps as a flavor enhancer, and I also like that it’s apple cider in an apple pie. It’s a nice symmetry,” she mentions.

Similarly, apple cider vinegar is used in the cooking liquid alongside sugar and butter to caramelize apples in a Classic Apple Tarte Tatin. The benefit is twofold: Vinegar’s acidity helps cut the sweetness of the caramel, and it prevents the apples from getting too mushy, instead maintaining their fork-tender texture.

Pastry chef and cookbook author Natasha Pickowicz often leans into the jolt vinegar can add, including adding a few drops to her cake soaks for an additional layer of flavor. “Cake soaks should have a balance of tart, sweet, and savory notes — just like vinaigrette for your favorite salad,” she writes in her cookbook More Than Cake. It can add intrigue to layered cakes like this Golden Spice Cake or Pumpkin Layer Cake. In her cookbook, she also calls for a glaze spiked with apple cider vinegar to brush onto an apple tart after baking. It’s the finishing touch “to further emphasize the tart’s resolute apple-ness,” she writes.

Apple cider vinegar doesn’t need to be limited to only apple desserts, either. In our Old-Fashioned Pecan Pie, we call for apple cider vinegar as a foil to the brown sugar filling’s cloying sweetness. A spoonful of apple cider vinegar may not announce itself boldly, but it makes a small splash for brighter, more balanced bakes.

Why You Need These AI Tools in 2025

Whether you're a social media influencer, marketer, or business owner, keeping up with the constant need for fresh, engaging content can be overwhelming. Let's Dive Into the Top 10 AI Tools for 2025

#9545. This Harvest Caesar Salad Is The Fall Side Everyone Asks Me To Bring

My love for Caesar salad knows no bounds, but in the fall, this harvest version is a STAPLE in my rotation. I first made it for a Friendsgiving last year, and people loved it so much that I ended up making it for my own Thanksgiving and Christmas celebrations, too. Every time, friends and family begged me for the recipe—it’s that good.

The best thing about it? It only requires a couple of easy ingredient upgrades to turn the classic salad into a fall favorite—here’s what makes it truly special.

As you’ve probably realized, this isn’t your plain Jane Caesar salad. There are two easy swaps that make this salad a side dish star. First, instead of romaine as the base, this salad lets kale shine. If you’re not a kale fan, stay with me. Once it’s massaged down with lemon juice and salt, it becomes perfectly tender and downright delicious—it’s the ideal hearty base for this salad.

The second and most important swap? Instead of sourdough croutons, this salad roasts pieces of butternut squash on a bed of freshly shredded Parm to create crispy frico squash “croutons.” As soon as I removed the tray from the oven and started breaking up the cheesy squash pieces, I had to remind myself that I couldn’t eat them all on their own—at least a few had to actually go in the salad.

This salad requires a few extra steps, but they’re quick and well worth it. First, make the Caesar dressing and refrigerate it until you’re ready to assemble. If you don’t have the time, a store-bought dressing will do just fine.

While that’s chilling, you’ll prepare the butternut squash croutons by cutting up your squash, shredding some Parm on an oiled baking sheet (don't use the pre-shredded kind—it just won’t melt the same), placing your squash on top, and baking until the cheese is crisp and browned on the bottom.

After you massage the kale with lemon and salt (don’t be stingy here—put those muscles to good use), all that’s left is to assemble! I highly recommend assembling in stages—dressing with the kale, then half the squash and Parmesan—before serving with the rest of the squash, Parmesan, and remaining dressing on the side for anyone who prefers more dressing than salad (again, guilty!).
